"I can't just write words that aren't in the book. That's making things up." He stared at the sentence until his eyes ached with a familiar fatigue. His brain felt dormant, like a toad waiting out winter. Then he remembered something. Last year, doing a social studies report, he had copied a quote from the textbook and seen odd little square marks inside it: "It [the canal] took ten years to build." He had thought the textbook made a mistake. Now he wasn't so sure.

He marched to the library, found the MLA handbook on the shelf behind the study carrels, and flipped through the pages until he found the section on quotations. There it was, plain as a field mouse. "In MLA style, square brackets go around any word a writer adds to a quotation, to show it was not in the original text." So the square brackets were not a mistake. They were a signal, a way of being honest and clear at the same time.

On Friday, Matthew stood up when Mrs. Okafor called his name. "The theme is that true friendship means slowing down for someone," he said, and read from his card: "He [Rat] would rather walk beside his friend than rush ahead alone." He held his breath.

Mrs. Okafor looked at the card for a long moment. Then she said, "Perfect," and copied it onto the board.

Priya poked him as he sat down. "You thought of that yourself?"

"Sort of," Matthew said, and turned the card over in his fingers. "I saw it once and thought it was wrong." He looked at the board, where his brackets sat there in green marker, small and square and exactly right.

Harper flopped onto her bed with her tablet balanced on her knees and opened the group chat called "Stats Nerds Unite." Three names glowed at the top: Priya, Marcus, and Jonah. Marcus had posted first, with a photo of his baseball card binder spread across the garage floor.

"Settling an argument with my cousin," Marcus had written. "David Justice or Derek Jeter, nineteen ninety-five and ninety-six. I say Justice both years. My cousin says Jeter."

Harper pulled up the numbers on her laptop while Priya typed "getting my notebook." The garage door slammed somewhere behind Marcus's next message, a blurry photo of his cousin holding a card like it owed him money. Justice was ahead in ninety-five, Harper confirmed, and ahead again in ninety-six. Case closed. She typed it, dropped the phone, and went to find a snack, feeling pleased with herself.

When she came back with a granola bar, the chat had deteriorated into chaos. Priya had added the two seasons together, and somehow, in both years where Justice beat Jeter, Jeter's combined average for the two years was higher. "That's bizarre," Harper said out loud to nobody. Marcus typed it faster: "That's bizarre and impossible, someone typed something wrong." Jonah sent a single skeptical eyeball emoji.

Priya's next message read like a tiny letter, and Harper read it twice:

"Dear everyone who is wrong, I did the math three times. Justice wins each year. Jeter wins the two years put together. My brother says look at how many times each of them batted, then look again. That's all I'm saying. Signed, Priya."

Harper set down her granola bar. At-bats. She scrolled back to her laptop and stared at the columns she'd copied earlier, the ones she'd skipped past because only the averages had seemed to matter. One player had batted a whole lot more times in one of those seasons, and the other had batted barely at all in it. She didn't say why it worked. She just tested it, dragging her finger down the at-bat column, then up again, checking each number like she was counting steps in the dark.

"Okay," she typed. "Priya's right. Look at the at-bats."

"I'm making a treaty," Marcus wrote back. "Nobody in this chat declares a winner of anything ever again without checking everything, not just the famous number." Priya replied, "Seconded," and Jonah sent a handshake emoji.

Then a new name appeared at the bottom of the chat, one Harper had never seen before: Marcus's cousin, added somehow, asking if they could settle a basketball argument next.

Muhammad held his candle like a torch and marched into the living room, where the whole family had gathered because the power had gone out for the whole street. "This is the third time this week," he announced, as if reporting news from a prestigious wire service. His older sister Layla groaned from the couch.

Ten minutes later, Muhammad crept to the kitchen and opened the refrigerator, letting its little bit of cold air spill over his face while he hunted for the yogurt. Layla caught him at it. "Again? You opened it five minutes ago!"

"I couldn't decide," Muhammad admitted. His conscience pinched him a little, because he knew she was right. Then Layla said something he had read on a fact sheet at school and never forgotten: "The USDA says a refrigerator keeps food safely cold for about four hours during a power cut, as long as the door stays closed." Muhammad stared at her, then at the fridge, doing the math. If the power had been out for one hour already, and he kept letting the cold out every five minutes, the four hours would shrink fast.

"So we get one opening," he said slowly. "One. We decide everything first, then open it once." He grabbed a pencil and wrote a note in the candlelight, which he read aloud with great ceremony: "Dear Fridge. Do not open. We are voting. Yogurt, grapes, or leftover rice. If you open this door before the family vote, you will retire from snack duty forever. Signed, Muhammad, Snack President." Layla laughed so hard she nearly dropped her candle.

They held the vote on the couch, everyone raising hands in the flickering light, grapes winning two to one. Then, together, they opened the fridge exactly once, grabbed the grapes, and shut it firmly. Muhammad taped his note to the door and saluted it. "Four hours," he whispered. "We can do this." Somewhere outside, a streetlight blinked back on, and the whole family booed, because now the vote had gone to waste.

The nurse with the green scissors looked up from the cast cutter. "Ready to see your arm again?"

Lydia had spent six weeks thinking about almost nothing else. She'd broken her left wrist in an acute fall from the monkey bars, and ever since, she'd been running little experiments inside the plaster. Every night she'd squeezed her fist tight, then loosened it, trying to simulate the exercises her right arm got all day lifting her backpack, brushing her teeth, dealing cards. "Ready," she said, and held still while the cutter buzzed.

When the two halves of the cast came apart, Lydia stared. Her left arm lay there pale and thin, with a shadowy line where the wrist had healed. She put both arms side by side on the exam table, and the difference was so strange it felt like an anomaly, as if the bones themselves had shrunk. "That's not mine," she said. "That's like a stick."

"It happens," said the nurse, easing her thumb gently along the healed line. "Muscles kept still in a cast weaken and shrink. That's why the arm looks thinner when the cast comes off."

"So all my squeezing did nothing?"

"You kept the fingers moving, which matters. Give me a squeeze now."

Lydia wrapped her hand around the nurse's fingers and pressed. Her grip felt soft, like fruit gone mealy. She tried again, harder, and her arm trembled halfway through.

"I have a whole plan," she said, watching the thin wrist bend. "Squeeze a ball at breakfast, carry the milk jug at dinner, measure both arms every Sunday until they match."

"You'll get there faster than you think." The nurse wrote something on a card and handed it over. "For your mom. It lists the exercises."

Lydia folded the card and slid it into her pocket, then flexed her fingers open, closed, open again. "Deal me in next card game," she told her brother. "Left hand. I need the practice."

Maya heard the plows before she heard her mother, and by the time she reached the kitchen in her socks, the radio had already said the words she wanted: no school, roads closed, snow day. She ate her cereal fast, then pulled on her boots, her coat, and her grandmother's dark wool mittens, the black ones with the reindeer around the wrist.

The backyard had turned into a white plateau, flat and level from the fence to the swing set, unmarked except for one line of rabbit tracks. Snow was still falling, small flakes drifting sideways in the wind. Maya held out one mitten and let a flake land on the dark wool. She leaned close and counted the arms with her eyes. Six. She caught another. Six again, this one thin and starry. A third flake landed, melted too fast to count, and a fourth sat there long enough for her to be sure. Six.

She tried a pale gray mitten next, and the flakes vanished into it before she could see anything. That gave her an idea, and she tested it: dark wool, easy to see; light wool, impossible. So the mittens mattered. But something else bothered her too. Every single flake had six arms, not five, not eight, and she wanted to know whether that was luck or a rule. She stood in the falling snow for a long time, catching flake after flake on the black mitten, keeping a tally in her head. Twelve flakes with six arms. Thirteen. Fourteen, and then her fingers got too cold to hold still.

Inside, her little brother Theo was at the kitchen table drawing snowflakes on paper with a silver marker. Maya looked over his shoulder and frowned. "Yours have eight points," she said. Theo shrugged and kept drawing. "It's a snowflake. Snowflakes have points."

"Not like that," Maya said. "I counted real ones outside. Snowflakes almost always have six sides or six arms." She held up the dark mitten. "It works better on this one. Catch them on something dark." Theo hesitated, then slid off his chair and pulled on his own coat, the one with the broken zipper, inside out so it would close.

They stood together on the plateau of the yard, and Maya showed him how to hold the mitten flat and low, out of the wind. Theo caught a big feathery one and bent over it, lips moving as he counted. "Six," he announced. He caught another. "Six." A third flake landed square in the middle of the wool and held its shape while they both stared at it, every arm perfect. "Okay," Theo said, breathing out a slow cloud of steam. "Show me the marker that isn't toxic anymore, the one Mom put by the sink. I'm starting over with my drawing."

The bank lobby smelled like paper and floor wax, and the stone wall outside the front doors was patched with gray lichen that Ethan had traced with one finger while he waited for his mother. She was refinancing something at the long counter, and she had told him to sit on the bench and finish his note cards, because his presentation was at two o'clock and it was already eleven. Two o'clock felt imminent. He flipped his cards and read them again: "Explain supply and demand using strawberries."

The trouble was that his cards only said that strawberries are cheap in summer and expensive in winter. That was true, but it wasn't an explanation, and his teacher had circled the word WHY on his rough draft in red pen. Ethan stared at the card. Cheap in summer, expensive in winter. He knew it from his grandmother's farm stand, and his mind went back there whether he wanted it to or not.

Last July, the stand's table had sagged under flats of strawberries, red to the point of being loud, and the price sign said two dollars a basket. In February, at the indoor market, the same basket cost six dollars, and there were only four baskets on the whole table. It had never struck him as strange until now. Lots of berries, low price. Few berries, high price. Then he remembered the strawberry lemonade, the summer his cousin Priya ran a stand and priced her fancy strawberry lemonade at five dollars a cup because the strawberries had cost so much at the winter market. By four o'clock she still had two full jugs. People wanted lemonade, but not at that price, and nobody bought it, and the extra lemonade just sat there. She had dumped it out at the curb, and the gutter had run pink.

Ethan grabbed a fresh card and wrote fast. If you hold the price up high, sellers will keep offering lots, but buyers only take a little, and what's left over piles up. He looked for a word for what was left over and remembered Priya yelling it at her mother that afternoon: "It's a surplus! We have a surplus!" He wrote "SURPLUS" in capital letters and underlined it twice.

"Ready?" His mother was standing over him with her purse on her shoulder.

"One more card," Ethan said. He wrote: "In winter the price is high because berries are few. In summer the price drops because berries are everywhere. And if a price stays too high, the extra just sits unsold." He squared the stack against his knee and stood up.

At the door he pushed the heavy brass handle, and the gray lichen caught the sunlight on the way out.

When Avery spotted the kitchen thermometer reading ten degrees Fahrenheit, she knew two things: school was cancelled, and the sledding hill would be perfect. She also noticed that the salt her dad had scattered on the front steps yesterday was just sitting there on top of the ice, doing absolutely nothing, like tiny white rocks on vacation.

"Weird," she said, crouching down. "Salt melts ice. It makes the water freeze at a colder temperature. So this should work." She flicked a few grains with her mitten. Nothing. She dashed inside and grabbed the outdoor thermometer, the one shaped like a duck, and pressed it against the porch rail. It settled at eleven degrees. Hmm. Her science notebook lay open on the hall table, and she read her own handwriting from a snowy experiment last winter: rock salt stops working well below about minus 10 degrees Celsius, which is 14 degrees Fahrenheit. Eleven was colder than fourteen. That was it. The salt wasn't broken; it was just too cold for salt to do its job.

To be sure, she drafted a quick message on a scrap of paper and taped it to the door for her little brother: EXPERIMENT IN PROGRESS. DO NOT STEP ON THE LEFT SIDE OF THE STEPS. SCIENCE THANKS YOU. Then she sprinkled fresh salt on the left steps only, drew a wobbly line down the middle with her boot, and marked the time in her notebook like a detective.

An hour later, after three runs down the hill on her saucer and one spectacular crash into a snowbank, she stomped back up the walk and inspected her crime scene. The right side of the steps, the untouched side, was solid ice under a thin layer of snow. The left side was bumpy and pocked, half-melted, with little tunnels where the salt had chewed through. She wrote it all down in what she called her intricate crime-scene formula: cold plus salt equals nothing, warmish plus salt equals slush. Her brother came out, read her note, and saluted her.

"Mad Scientist Avery," he said, "your steps are weird and slushy."

"That's called evidence," she said, and flicked a salt grain at him.

Wyatt crouched beside the camp stove, turning the sausages with a fork while his little sister Nora arranged the paper plates in a row and named them like prizes. She wanted to be the one who served dinner tonight, and she had told everyone at the lake that afternoon until Dad laughed and promised her the job. Wyatt had promised something too: the meal itself, fried sausage and toasted buns, all cooked by him without any help.

The oil in the pan popped once, twice, then flared. A ribbon of orange crawled across the surface and licked up the side, and suddenly half the pan was flickering. Wyatt's hand shot toward the water bottle by his knee, because water was what you threw on fire, and then he stopped. Two summers ago, at his uncle's cookout, he had watched a frying pan do exactly this, and his uncle had not reached for the hose. He had slid a lid over the flames instead, calm as anything, and the fire had gone out like someone had pinched its nose shut.

"Turn it off," Wyatt said out loud, to himself as much as to Nora, and he shut off the stove knob with a click. Then he grabbed the lid from the picnic table and slid it over the pan, angling it so the flames couldn't slip past the rim. The fire underneath fought for a second, then died. Nora peeked around his elbow.

"You didn't put water on it," she said.

"Never pour water on a grease fire," Wyatt said. "It has to be the lid."

He lifted the corner of the lid a minute later, checking. The sausages were browned, not burnt, and steam curled up in a thin white vapor that smelled like breakfast even though it was almost sunset. Dad came back from the woodpile with his arms full and stopped when he saw the lid.

"Little trouble?" Dad asked.

"A flare-up," Wyatt said. "I remembered Uncle Rob's pan. Lid on, heat off. Worked."

Dad set down the wood and looked at Wyatt for a moment, the way he did when a kid did something that wasn't kid-sized. "You want to elaborate on that plan for me?"

"You can't use water on burning oil. Water spreads it everywhere. But if you cut off the heat and cover it, the fire runs out of what it needs." Wyatt flipped the sausages onto a plate. "It's like the fire has rules. Once you know them, it's not scary, it's just probable. Flare-up, lid, done."

Nora lifted the plate high and marched it to the picnic table, announcing dinner to the trees. Wyatt followed with the toasted buns, and Dad said, "Same cook tomorrow?" and Wyatt was already planning pancakes.

The pharmacy smelled like mint and hand sanitizer, and Isla stood in the deodorant aisle holding her phone like evidence. On the screen was a text from her best friend, Nadia: "People were moving away from you in gym today. You didn't notice?" Isla had noticed. She had also noticed that she'd skipped her shower after Tuesday's practice, and after Wednesday's, because the locker room was crowded and she'd been in a hurry. She grabbed a stick of deodorant and read the back like it might confess something.

Behind the counter, the pharmacist was ringing up a man's cough syrup. Two women by the vitamins were having a quiet argument about whether the new pharmacy hours were fair, and one of them said the whole thing had become a controversy at the neighborhood meeting. Isla wasn't listening. She was thinking. Nadia had said the smell got worse as class went on, which meant the deodorant she'd swiped on that morning should have still been working. Unless the problem wasn't the start of the day. Unless it was all the sweat and the running around in between, sitting there on her skin hour after hour.

She put the deodorant back on the shelf and walked home fast, went straight into the bathroom, and showered with soap, scrubbing everywhere, twice. Then she did an experiment on herself. Thursday she showered with soap after practice. Friday she skipped it and used extra deodorant instead. Thursday, nobody edged away; Nadia even shared her popcorn. Friday, three kids drifted to the far side of the bleachers, and Isla, trying not to be pessimistic, told herself maybe the wind was blowing the wrong way. It wasn't the wind.

"Body odor is sweat plus bacteria," Isla announced at dinner, "and soap washes both away." Her little brother made a face. "That's why I'm not skipping after practice anymore. I checked with my own nose."

"Your own nose can't smell you," her brother said.

Isla paused, fork in the air. She looked down at her gym bag by the door, sitting there since Tuesday, never once unpacked, and stood up.

Hudson had exactly forty minutes to solve the last clue on the science center's field trip sheet, and the clue made no sense. It read: "Find the spotted guard who never rode." His pencil hovered over the blank line while his classmates stormed the gift shop like it was under siege, pressing against the glass until the clerk looked ready to call for backup.

Mr. Alvarez, the frugal chaperone who had handed out exactly one token per kid and not one more, tapped his watch. "Twenty minutes, then we regroup at the bus." Priya slid up beside Hudson, holding her own sheet with five of six blanks filled. "Guard who never rode," she said. "Armor hall? The knight exhibit?" She wanted the free pass to the robotics lab that came with a perfect sheet. Hudson wanted it too, but mostly he wanted to figure the thing out, because last month he'd skipped the puzzle table at his cousin's party and regretted it ever since. He wasn't skipping this one.

The halls branched three ways. Down one corridor, a prism display shot rainbows across the ceiling, and Priya paused to watch the light refract into separate colors. "Focus," Hudson said, though he almost didn't. Then he noticed the sign at the end of the corridor: Fire Safety Hall. "Guard," he said. "Like a guard dog."

Inside, an old hand-pumped engine sat behind a rope, and beside it hung a painting of a white dog covered in black spots. A younger kid from another school pointed at it. "Why is there a dog picture next to a firetruck?" His teacher shrugged and steered him toward the smoke detector display.

Hudson studied the wall instead. There was a faded photograph of the same kind of engine being pulled by a team of horses, and out in front of the horses, small and blurry, ran a spotted dog. Another photo showed the dog trotting alongside a horse like the two were old friends. Hudson felt something click, the way the prism had split one beam into colors you couldn't see before. The dog never rode. It ran. Ahead.

"It's a Dalmatian," he said, writing fast. "Dalmatians became firehouse dogs because they got along well with horses, and they ran ahead of the horse-drawn fire carriages, helping clear the way." Priya squinted at the photo, then at the painting, then copied his answer, which meant she'd gotten it from him, and they both knew it.

"So who gets the robotics pass?" she asked as the group gathered by the bus.

Hudson looked at the pass in the teacher's hand, then at Priya's stubborn, hopeful face. "Flip you for it," he said, and pulled a coin from his jacket pocket.

Noah burst through the kitchen door still wearing his boots, sending a spray of snow across the tiles. "It's a snow day! A real one!" He skidded to the counter and grabbed his mom's phone before she could say a word. On the weather app, the temperature read twenty-one degrees, but right below it sat a second number, and it made him frown. "It says it feels like nine degrees. Nine! How can it feel like nine when it's twenty-one?"

His little sister Marisol peered over his elbow, nose red from the yard. "Maybe your phone's broken," she said.

Noah scrolled, but the numbers stayed the same. Twenty-one. Feels like nine. He stomped back outside to test it himself, because that was what you did with a mystery. The air in the corner behind the shed, where the fence blocked the breeze, actually felt almost pleasant. He could stand there in his coat and think about the mountains of snow waiting for him. But the moment he stepped into the open middle of the yard, the wind found him, and the cold bit through his gloves like it had teeth.

"So it's the wind," he said out loud, marching between the two spots twice more to be sure. Behind the shed, comfortable. Open yard, freezing. Same sky, same snow, same twenty-one degrees. He cupped his hands around his mouth and shouted toward the house. "Marisol! Come feel this!"

She came, boots squeaking, and he walked her between the two spots like a tour guide. "Notice anything?"

"It's freezing out here and warm back there." She rubbed the tip of her ear, which had gone from pink to an angry red. "Wait. Is that why the phone has that other number? The wind one?"

"The wind chill," Noah said. "That's what it's called. The wind makes cold air feel colder." He pointed at the app, and Marisol's eyes went wide when she saw the gap between twenty-one and nine.

They got to work. Noah nominated the spot behind the shed as base camp for the day's operations, and Marisol seconded the motion instantly, since it was the only place where her ears stopped aching. From there they rolled the fattest snowball either of them had ever built, and by noon they had a snowman with a scarf, a bottle-cap nose, and two lumps of coal they'd traded a bag of pretzels for through the fence to the neighbor kid.

Noah patted the snowman's round belly. "We should nominate you for mayor," he said.

"His name is Lumpkin," Marisol announced, and stuck a stick arm straight up into the wind.

Hunter wanted the last open basketball court before anyone else could claim it, but Marcus was already standing at the free throw line with the ball under his arm. They agreed to shoot for it, except the hoop's net was gone and the rim was bent, so neither of them could trust a fair shot. Marcus shook the rock he always threw first and said, "Rock wins. That's just how it goes."

Hunter had lost to that rock three times this week, and he began to perceive a pattern in how Marcus played. Marcus never varied. He believed rock was strongest the way some kids believe a lucky sock wins games, and he treated every loss as bad luck rather than a broken idea. Hunter picked paper, of course, and won, and Marcus demanded a rematch, and then another, throwing rock every single time. After the third loss, Marcus sat down hard on the hot rubber ground and stared at the chalk dust on his sneakers.

"Watch," Hunter said, and he drew three quick circles in the dust with a stick. Rock beats scissors and loses to paper. Paper beats rock and loses to scissors. Scissors beats paper and loses to rock. Each one won against exactly one other and lost to exactly one. "See? Rock isn't stronger," he said. "None of them is better than the others." Marcus squinted at the circles for a long moment, then laughed, mostly at himself, and Hunter thought his laugh sounded lighter than usual.

They still needed a rule for the court, so Hunter pulled a folded note from his pocket, a message from his older sister: "If you both want the same thing, say what the problem is out loud, then pick a rule neither of you can cheat." Hunter read it aloud. The problem, they agreed out loud, was that they both wanted the court and both had won some of the ties. The fair rule they chose was alternating halves, winner keeps playing, loser gets next game, every single day, no exceptions. It was a versatile rule, one that would work for basketball, foursquare, or the swings in the morning before school.

Marcus handed over the ball as testimony of his surrender, his palm leaving a print in the chalk dust, and said, "Tomorrow I'm throwing scissors." Hunter spun the ball on one finger and replied, "Tomorrow I'll finally have no idea what you'll throw."

Evan had been waiting all week for the Sato family reunion at his aunt's house, mostly because of one thing: Aunt Mariko's ramen. He'd watched videos about it, and he'd even practiced with chopsticks at home using dry spaghetti, which his cat, Biscuit, kept stealing off the floor.

When he arrived, the greetings started immediately. On his mom's side, everyone hugged. On the Sato side, Aunt Mariko bowed slightly, so Evan bowed back, a little too deep, and nearly knocked over a lamp. Everyone laughed, and his cousin Kenji gave him two thumbs up. Kenji pressed a small wrapped box into Evan's hands. "For you. Don't open it yet, that part comes later," Kenji said. Evan clutched it like treasure. In his own house, gifts got ripped open on the spot, so waiting felt like holding a sneeze in.

Then came the ramen, steaming in huge bowls, and Evan's plan exploded. Everyone slurped. Aunt Mariko slurped. Grandpa Sato slurped so loudly it sounded like a drain unclogging. Evan froze with his chopsticks halfway up. At home, one tiny slurp meant a look from his grandmother that could diminish a person's appetite entirely. He glanced around the table, testing his idea: maybe here, the noise meant something good. He slurped one noodle, cautiously, like a scientist. Aunt Mariko beamed. "There it is!" she said. Kenji leaned over and whispered, "In Japan, slurping noodles like ramen and soba is acceptable at the table. It's not rude here." Evan slurped again, louder, and Grandpa Sato laughed and slurped back, like they were having a conversation in noodle language.

Between bites, Evan noticed his own bias had been the problem: he'd assumed one set of table manners was the only set. He also noticed Uncle Tadao served himself exactly one modest scoop of everything, frugal as ever, while Uncle Pete from Evan's side took enough for three people. Two families, one table, completely different rulebooks, and somehow it all worked.

Later, finally allowed to open his gift, Evan peeled the paper slowly and found a red ramen bowl with a dragon on it. "So you can practice at home," Kenji said. Evan held it up, grinned, and took his biggest slurp of the night, right out of the empty bowl.

Megan sat cross-legged on her bed with her notebook open to a page titled "The Mystery." For months she had been collecting clues: the new shoes she needed in August, the two inches she had grown since spring, the way her mood could flip like a light switch for no reason she could see. Something invisible was running a schedule inside her, and she wanted to know the rules. Tonight her plan was a chart, because charts had helped her figure out her bean plants in science. Seeds germinate when the conditions line up, and she suspected her body worked the same way, on some hidden timetable she couldn't watch directly. Her hypothesis had germinated at Priya's house on Saturday, when Priya had flopped onto the rug and said, "My sister got her first period when she was ten. Ten! And she's still mad about it."

Megan had blinked. "My sister was fourteen. That's a huge difference."

"I know," Priya said. "I asked my mom, and she said a big CDC survey in the United States found the median age is about twelve, but with a wide normal range around it. So basically anywhere near that is normal."

Back in her bedroom now, Megan wrote TEN on a sticky note and FOURTEEN on another and stuck them on her wall, with TWELVE, MEDIAN in the middle. Median, she knew from math, meant the middle value, the one in the center when you lined everybody up. So ten and fourteen were both inside a wide range around twelve, like two houses on opposite ends of the same long street. That was her test: if the pattern held, then there was no single right age, and the flips and the new shoes and everything else were just the street she lived on. She texted Priya her theory, then pulled up the email Priya had sent that afternoon, because Priya had a project of her own going.

"Dear Megan," it read. "I'm making a poster for my cousin's birthday. She's turning thirteen soon and she's nervous she's 'late.' I want to tell her the survey thing but in a fun way, not a lecture. Can you draw me a timeline with shoes on it? You're better at drawing than me. Also my sister says hi. Your friend, Priya."

Megan grinned, and the grin felt contagious, like it spread all by itself to the pencil in her hand. She drew a long street with houses from ten to fourteen, put a big star on the middle of the block, and labeled each house with a different girl. Then she photographed it and hit send.

Two minutes later her phone buzzed: "PERFECT. My sister says she wants one for her wall too."

Megan taped her sticky notes in a neat row above her desk, stepped back, and nodded at her wall. "Wide normal range," she said out loud, and clicked off the lamp.

Ella's little brother Theo banged his fork against his glass like a tiny judge with a gavel. "The bridge is flooded," he announced, holding up Mom's phone. "Tanya says the whole road to Grandma's is underwater. Look." The photo on the screen showed brown water swallowing a guardrail, waves distinct against the gray sky. Mom leaned in, her spoon of soup paused halfway to her mouth. She had promised to drive to Grandma's on Saturday to help her restock her freezer, and Grandma had been asking about the visit all week.

"Send it to me," Ella said, already pulling out her own phone under the table, which was allowed at dinner only for emergencies. Theo slid the phone across the tablecloth, nearly into the gravy boat. Ella remembered a day two summers ago when Theo had fallen off his bike and split his chin; he'd sat at this same table while Mom gently felt the curve of her own jaw and told him the hard part there was cartilage, and that his would heal. He trusted facts he could feel. But a flood photo was different. You couldn't feel where it came from.

"That's it," Ella said suddenly, standing up so fast her chair scraped. "A reverse image search can show where a photo appeared online before." She walked the photo into the search, fingers quick, while Theo hovered at her elbow. The results loaded, and there it was: the same guardrail, the same brown water, on a news site from years back. The photo was real, but it was old, being passed off as new. "Someone's recycling it," Ella said. "That doesn't mean today's flood is fake, but this picture isn't proof."

Mom exhaled and set down her spoon. "So I call the county road line in the morning instead of panicking tonight." She reached over and smoothed Theo's cowlick, which had been mimicking a rooster's comb all through dinner. Theo frowned at the screen, then brightened. "Wait. Can it find where that shark photo came from too? The one Marcus said was at the beach?"

Ella grinned and pulled up the shark.

Elliot set his fork down and stared at his sister Maya, who was grinning across the meatloaf like she had won something. "Bree made the team bulletin board," Maya said, sliding her phone across the table. "Perfect shooting percentage. One hundred percent. Coach printed it out and everything."

"That's amazing," Mom said from the stove, where the kitchen felt tranquil and warm, insulated from the cold rattling the window outside.

Elliot looked at the number. It glowed there, 100%, like it was made of gold. From his perspective, sitting at the far end of the table, it almost looked too clean. Last season flashed back to him, one rainy Saturday when he had gone to watch Maya's game. He remembered every girl taking shot after shot, misses raining down like the rain outside, and he remembered Bree on the bench the whole game except for one play near the end, when the ball happened to land in her hands.

"How many shots has Bree taken?" he asked.

Maya shrugged. "The board doesn't say."

"So you don't know if it's one out of one, or ten out of ten, or fifty out of fifty."

"It says one hundred percent. That's all that matters." Maya grabbed her phone back.

Elliot pushed his chair in and walked to the hallway where his sneakers sat. "Come on," he said. "The stats notebook is in the gym office. Coach lets us look at it."

They walked the six blocks in the dark, and Maya got quieter with every step, which Elliot took as a good sign. In the office, under the desk lamp, he flipped the notebook to Bree's row and ran his finger along it. Field goals attempted: one. Field goals made: one.

"One shot," Elliot said. "She took one shot the whole season."

Maya stared at the page. "She's going to kill me if I tell everyone."

"Tell her to keep shooting first," Elliot said, and closed the notebook.

Ms. Rivera's science cabinet was notorious for eating equipment, so Lauren had to negotiate with Marcus for the last working lamp while he was still untangling its cord. "You can have it Tuesday," Marcus said. "I need it now," Lauren said, holding up a Styrofoam ball. "I'm proving my cousin wrong before he texts me again."

Last night her cousins had argued over video call until Grandma told them to hush. "The Moon's getting bigger this week," Dante had insisted. "It's shrinking," Priya had shot back. "It looked fatter yesterday." Lauren had said "I don't know" at the time, and it had bugged her ever since, like a pebble in her shoe.

She set the lamp in the middle of the darkened science room and stuck the ball onto a ruler, a quick adaptation of a proper orbit model, since the stand for it had gone missing sometime around the Ice Age. Priya's friend Zoe held the lamp steady while Lauren walked the ball in a slow circle. From where they stood, only half the ball ever caught the light, but the lit slice they could see changed as it went around.

"There," Zoe said, when the ball neared the far side of its circle. "From here it looks like a little fingernail."

Lauren walked the ball onward and the bright part grew, night by night, position by position, until it was nearly full. "Waxing," she said out loud. "That's the word for when the lit part grows. So Dante was right, this week the Moon is waxing." Then she kept walking the circle, and the lit part began to shrink, sliver by sliver. "And waning is the opposite. Priya will be right in two weeks. They're both right, just at different times."

She grabbed her phone and typed fast: come over Saturday, bring Dante, I have a lamp and a ball and you're both going to lose the argument.

Evelyn pressed her badge against the glass case marked Fungus Lights, where ghostly mushrooms glowed faint green, and wished her circuit at the workbench glowed at all. She had a battery, a switch, a bulb and three wires, plus a worksheet with one question: Why does the bulb light? Her partner Marisol had wandered off to the prism wall, where the afternoon sun refracted through the triangles and threw rainbow stripes across the floor, so Evelyn was alone with the parts that refused to work.

She clipped the wires, snapped the switch closed, and got nothing. She flipped the switch open, then closed again, slower this time, watching the little metal arm touch its contact. Nothing. The problem had to be somewhere she couldn't see, inside the flow itself, and that was the maddening part. She checked the battery, positive to positive. She tightened every clip until her thumbs ached. Then she held the last wire against the bulb's side with her finger instead of the clip, and the bulb blazed on so suddenly she gasped.

The clip was bad. The connection, not the battery, had been the hidden trouble all along. When Marisol came back trailing rainbow light on her sleeves, Evelyn was already drawing on the worksheet. "Look, we need two bulbs for the next part," Marisol said. "If one breaks, everything goes dark, right? Like last time at school." Evelyn hesitated, then remembered the case at the entrance, the two glowing mushroom patches that stayed bright even though the sign said one patch had gone out. She sketched fast, splitting the wires so each bulb had its own path back to the battery instead of sharing one.

"A parallel circuit," Marisol read off the sign above the next bench, grinning.

They unscrewed one bulb to test it. The other bulb kept burning, steady and bright.

"Told you," Evelyn said, and switched them both off and on again, just to watch.

The marble hallway of the courthouse smelled like floor polish, and Joshua's note cards were sweating in his hand. His class was holding a mock committee hearing in a real courtroom, and each student had to explain how a bill becomes a law. Joshua's problem was smaller and stranger: the handout from their teacher kept calling the school-safety proposal "the School Safety Bill" in one paragraph and "the School Safety Act" in another. Same proposal, two different names, and nobody seemed to think that was weird.

"Maybe it's a typo," whispered Priya as they waited outside the courtroom doors.

Joshua didn't think so. The pattern was too tidy. Every time the handout mentioned the proposal being introduced, debated, or voted on, it said bill. Every time it mentioned the thing after the final vote, it said Act. He tested the idea in the margin, writing a small B next to the early mentions and a small A next to the later ones. The letters split perfectly at the moment of passage. The name changed when the proposal crossed the finish line.

When his turn came, Judge Marquez, an influential volunteer who ran these hearings every spring, asked him to walk the class through the stages. Joshua decomposed the process on the whiteboard, step by step: introduction, committee, debate, votes in both chambers. Then he stopped at the last box he had drawn.

"This is where it confused me," he said, tapping the marker against the board. "It's called a bill until it passes all its stages. Once it passes, it's not a bill anymore. It's an Act."

"So it's like a caterpillar and a butterfly," Priya called out. "Same creature, different name depending on the stage."

Judge Marquez smiled and turned to the class. "Mr. Speaker, I move we vote on the amendment." Every hand went up, and the gavel came down with a crack that made even the bailiff jump.

Naomi had noticed it for a month without saying anything. Every day at lunch, her classmate Yusuf pushed his tray away untouched, and every afternoon he looked tired by last period. She had a theory, but theories about people were tricky, so she kept a list in her notebook: Monday, no pizza. Tuesday, no sandwich. Wednesday, he even skipped the chocolate pudding, which nobody skipped.

On Saturday morning her mother dropped her at the community hall with a plate of frosted cookies and one instruction. "The gift table closes at noon, so hand those in before the games start." The hall was already full. Streamers hung from the ceiling fans, and a line of aunties arranged platters of samosas and dates on a long table near the stage. Naomi recognized Yusuf near the front, wearing a white kurta she had never seen before, standing with his grandmother.

"You're here," he said. "This is Eid al-Fitr. It means Ramadan is over, the month when Muslims fast from dawn until sunset." He picked up a date and ate it, and Naomi watched him do it the way a scientist watches a test succeed. That explained the tray. That explained the tiredness. From her perspective, the whole month of school slid into place like a puzzle she had been holding upside down.

Then the problem arrived. Yusuf's little sister had entered the cookie-decorating contest, and the entry box shut at noon, but she was stuck at the back of a line for the bathroom. Naomi counted heads, counted minutes, and made a decision: she surrendered her own contest entry, slid her frosting tube and sprinkle jar across the table to the sister, and ran the plate of cookies to the gift table with the clock on the wall showing four minutes to twelve. Behind her, the judges called for last entries just as the girl's cookie landed in the box.

Afterward, sitting on folding chairs with paper plates balanced on their knees, Yusuf asked whether it had bothered her, guessing wrong for a month. "I thought maybe the cafeteria food was controversial at your house," Naomi said. He laughed so hard he nearly dropped his samosa. "You could have just asked." She pulled out her notebook, crossed out every line on the list, and wrote one word at the bottom: solved. Then she took a bite of his grandmother's biryani and asked for seconds.

John pressed his back against the cool plaster wall of Ms. Prieto's studio and sang his part of the round for the ninth time. The song was "The Emperor's New Melody," a silly tune Ms. Prieto had written herself, and the whole choir would perform it in two-part harmony at the spring concert. That was the problem. Every time Marisol started the high part, John's low part slid right up after it like a lost dog following the wrong owner.

"You did it again," Marisol said, lowering her sheet music. "You're singing my note."

"I am not." John scrutinized the page as if the answer might be hiding between the staff lines. "I'm singing a G. It says G."

They tried it again, and again John's voice climbed, and Marisol laughed so hard she snorted, which made him laugh too, and Ms. Prieto tapped her tuning fork on the edge of the piano.

"Lessons are over in ten minutes," she said, "and this harmony is becoming controversial. Half the parents will text me if it sounds like a car alarm." She settled onto the piano bench with her coffee. "Figure it out, you two."

John hummed his G. Then, out of pure stubbornness, he hummed Marisol's note, the one that kept stealing his voice. He hummed them one after the other, back and forth, and squinted at the piano keys like they owed him money. Something itched at him. The two notes didn't clash at all. They sounded like the same note, just one tall and one short, like the same kid standing on a chair.

"Play a G," he told Ms. Prieto, "and then the next G up." She did, and John grinned. "Marisol. We're both singing G. Yours is just higher. Same note, different heights." She tested it against the piano, and her eyebrows went up.

"So when I follow you," John said, talking it through with his hands, "I'm not really leaving my part. I'm climbing up to your height, because my ear thinks the same note should sound the same. But it doesn't have to." He remembered a diagram from a book in the library, wavy lines rising and doubling. "That high one vibrates twice as fast as mine. Exactly twice. That's why they match."

Ms. Prieto set her coffee down slowly. "Nobody taught you that today."

"The library did."

They sang it one more time. John kept his G low and steady, and when Marisol's high G floated in above it, his voice held firm, locked to the floor like a good anchor. The two notes stacked together, warm and shivery, and Ms. Prieto didn't say anything at all, just closed the piano lid with a soft click.

"Encore," whispered Marisol, and started them off again.

The score was stuck at one. Oliver leaned closer to Maya's basement computer, where a little conductor sprite in a blue hat was supposed to award a point every time the player's train caught a falling coin, and the score had gone up exactly once, on the very first coin, and never again.

"You need a loop," Maya said, spinning her desk chair around. "Right now your script runs one time and quits, like it's clocking out." She popped the cap off a marker and drew a circle on the whiteboard her dad kept down there. "Everything inside this circle happens over and over until you say stop."

Oliver dragged a "repeat until" block out of the purple Control drawer and snapped it around his coin script. He tested it, and the coin fell, and fell, and kept falling straight off the bottom of the screen forever. "Okay, that's a problem," he admitted, laughing. The loop worked, but nothing told the coin to go back to the top and try again. He added an "if then" block: if the coin touched the conductor's net, add one to score, then move the coin back up. If it missed and hit the floor, back up anyway, no point. He clicked the green flag and held his breath.

One. Two. Three. The score climbed every single catch. Oliver pumped both fists and nearly knocked over Maya's stack of library books. "Four! Maya, it's working, it's actually keeping score!" He wanted to integrate a timer next, and maybe a level where the coins fell faster, and he started stacking blocks so fast the program looked like a rainbow had exploded.

Footsteps came down the basement stairs. It was Maya's grandpa, carrying a plate of crackers. He set it down and peered at the screen over their shoulders, his eyebrows climbing. "You two are writing a computer program? Where's all the code? The walls of numbers and letters, like in the movies?"

"There aren't any," Oliver said. "You just snap blocks together, like LEGO." He dragged a block out, snapped it back in, and the whole script glowed blue for a second.

Grandpa shook his head slowly, delighted and confused at the same time. "Who thought of that?"

"It's called Scratch," Maya said. "It came out of the MIT Media Lab, back in 2007."

"Blocks that code," Grandpa said, mostly to himself. "My whole career in the signal corps, and now an eleven-year-old builds a game by clicking pieces together." He tapped the edge of the monitor. "Is that laptop of yours durable? Because you're going to be at this for a while."

"He's not getting it back until I beat his high score," Maya said.

Oliver cracked his knuckles, moved the "when green flag clicked" hat block to the top, and grinned at the screen. "Ready, conductor?"

Noah had spent forty minutes looking for the Moon the night before, and he hadn't found it anywhere. "Maybe it vanished," his little sister had said, and even though he knew that was silly, he couldn't say why. So when Ms. Ruiz set a lamp in the middle of the science room and announced that today they would illustrate the Moon's phases, Noah sat up fast.

She darkened the windows, switched on the lamp, and told them the lamp was the Sun. Each pair got a styrofoam ball on a stick. "Earth is your head," she said. "Walk your Moon around it and watch what happens." Noah partnered with Priya, who held her ball up like a lollipop and spun in a circle just to make people laugh.

Noah kept his ball slow and steady. Halfway around, he stopped. From where he stood, the ball was between his head and the lamp, and the lit side of the ball faced completely away from him. His side looked dark, like nothing at all. He turned his head carefully. If he was Earth, he realized, he would be staring at the unlit half of the Moon straight on. "Priya," he whispered, "come look from my spot."

Priya squinted into the dark half of the ball. "It's invisible," she said. "Like it vanished."

"That's what happened last night," Noah said. His mind was racing through it. At new moon, the Moon lies roughly between Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us, and it looks dark. He hadn't lost the Moon. It had been out there, dark, hidden in the Sun's general direction, which was also why he couldn't see it well after sunset. "I thought something was wrong with the sky. It wasn't an anomaly. It was supposed to happen."

"You mean new moon?" Priya asked.

"That's the one." Noah walked his ball a quarter turn farther, and a thin bright crescent curled into view along its edge. Then a half. He kept circling, and the lit part kept growing, until the whole face near the lamp side glowed round and white. Priya copied him, calling out each shape: crescent, half, full. When Noah reached the dark spot between Earth and Sun again, he made his ball pause there on purpose, the way you'd check a math answer by redoing it.

Ms. Ruiz walked past their table and watched the dark ball pass through the space between Noah's head and the lamp. "Nice pacing," she said, and moved on.

At lunch, Priya leaned across the table. "So last night it was somewhere near new moon?"

"Roughly between us and the Sun, dark side toward us," Noah said, tearing his bread in half to demonstrate, one piece bright under the window, one shadowed in his palm. "Tonight I'm going to find it anyway. There's a thin one coming in a couple of days, low in the west after sunset."

Priya pointed at the shadowed piece of bread in his hand. "Show me that crescent part one more time."

The library meeting room smelled like old carpet and lemon cleaner, and folding chairs squeaked every time someone shifted. Rose sat in the front row with nine other spellers, her number pinned to her shirt, waiting for the librarian at the microphone to call her name. She had studied word lists all month, and she had sorted the words into groups in her notebook to make them easier to remember, deciding she could categorize them by language of origin, which helped her guess at letters she wasn't sure of.

The first rounds went quickly. A boy from her school got out on "buoyant." A sixth grader spelled "melancholy" with calm, slow certainty. Then the librarian said, "Rose, your word is 'chandelier.'"

Rose stepped up to the microphone. "Chandelier. C-H-A-N-D-E-L-I-E-R." She paused before the last syllable because something felt wrong, a small itch at the back of her mind. The judge was already reaching for the bell.

"Wait," Rose said. "Can I start over?"

The librarian glanced at the judge, who nodded. "You may start your word again," the librarian said, "but if you change any letters you've already said, that counts as a misspelling."

Rose stood very still. So she could say the whole word again, but she could not quietly fix a letter she had already spoken. If she said "C-H-A-N" again, it had to be "C-H-A-N." She tried to remember exactly what she had said the first time. C. H. A. N. D. E. L. Then it came to her: the ending was the trouble. She had been about to spell it like the end of "carrier," but the word came from French, and in her notebook French endings were the ones that liked an extra letter.

"Chandelier," she said again. "C-H-A-N-D-E-L-I-E-R. Chandelier."

"Correct," the librarian said, and Rose walked back to her seat with her hands still shaking a little.

In the next round the word was "vessel," which felt almost too easy after chandelier. "Vessel. V-E-S-S-E-L. Vessel." She got to watch the boy beside her go out on "genuine," and she felt bad for him, but she also noticed something: the words that knocked people out were ones where the spelling looked arbitrary, like the letters had been arranged by someone rolling dice.

Only Rose and the calm sixth grader, Priya, were left. The librarian looked at her card, then at the two girls, and said, "Rose, your word is 'privilege.'"

Rose stepped to the microphone. "Privilege. P-R-I-V-I..." She stopped. She had said the wrong vowel, and she knew it, and she knew that no matter how many times she started over, she could not take that "I" back.

"Privilege," she said. "P-R-I-V-I-L-E-G-E. Privilege."

The judge rang the bell, once, softly. Priya won the little plastic trophy, and afterward she came over and said, "You almost had it." Rose looked at the trophy, then at her own shoes, and said, "Same word next year."

Olivier slouched at the lunch table, staring at the translucent plastic sleeve that held his baseball card of Ted Williams. The card had cost him three weeks of allowance, and now Marcus was telling everyone it was worthless because old players could not hit anymore.

"It's not about old players," Olivier said. "It's about the number. Look at the back."

Marcus grabbed the card. "Four oh six? What's that supposed to mean?"

"It means he got a hit about four times out of every ten," said Priya, who was sorting the class survey data into one category for basketball fans and another for baseball fans. "My grandpa talks about it constantly. He bets people that nobody has hit .400 since before he was born, and he wins every time."

Olivier sat up. "Since before he was born? How old is he?"

"Seventy-nine. He says the last one was Ted Williams, .406, in 1941. Nobody in Major League Baseball has finished a whole season above .400 since then."

Marcus frowned at the card. "So the card is good?"

"The card is good," Olivier said, but something else was bothering him. Priya's grandfather bet people and won. That meant most fans believed somebody had done it recently. Olivier decided to test it. At lunch the next day he walked the cafeteria with a notebook and asked eleven kids the same question: has anyone hit .400 in a big-league season lately? Nine said yes, and six of them named players Olivier could check. That evening he looked up each name and wrote the real numbers beside the guesses. Nobody was close.

On Friday, Olivier asked Mr. Delgado if he could supervise a short presentation during current events, since averages and percentages were already on the agenda. He stood at the front holding the Williams card and read out his eleven answers next to the facts. "One number hides a hundred games," he said. "That's why people get it wrong."

Marcus raised his hand. "Okay. So what do you want for the card?"

"Forty dollars," said Olivier.

"Ten."

"Twenty-five, and I keep the sleeve."

The third dryer rumbled to life just as Mya's mother handed her a ten dollar bill and a short list written on the back of a dryer sheet. "Milk, and nothing from the candy rack," her mother said, already turning back to the laundry baskets. "You know the way. Corner store, two blocks, left on Pine." Mya stood there for a second, holding the bill like it might chirp. Last summer she had been allowed only as far as the mailbox. Now she was being sent out into the world with money and a mission.

Walking the two blocks took less stamina than she'd expected, though her legs felt hesitant at the corner of Pine, where she had to wait for a car that turned out to be going much slower than it looked. She remembered the time she'd begged to go to the store with her older cousin and been told no, and how she'd cried about it for an hour. She winced a little at the memory. Maybe being kept home hadn't been an insult. Maybe it had just been a door that opened late.

The store smelled like cardboard and oranges. In the dairy cooler she found the milk and then stopped, because there were choices. One two-litre carton for $3.49, or one-litre cartons for $1.89 each. Her list said "2 litres," so two small ones would do it. She reached for the small cartons, then paused. Beneath the big price stickers, in smaller print, there were more numbers: $1.74 per litre on the big carton, $1.89 per litre on the small. She leaned closer, checking that she was reading it right.

"Unit price," said the man behind the counter, without looking up from his crossword. "It's printed right there." Mya nodded slowly. So the big carton was cheaper per litre, which meant she'd save fifteen cents a litre if she bought it. She did the math on her fingers: $3.49 versus $3.78. Twenty-nine cents. Twenty-nine cents was a piece of gum, roughly.

But then she checked the shelf one row down, where the chocolate milk sat, and noticed something that made her frown. The big carton of chocolate milk said $2.15 per litre, and the small one said $2.10 per litre. The bigger carton was more per litre, not less. So bigger wasn't always cheaper. The rule she'd just discovered had a hole in it, and somehow that made the whole thing more interesting, not less. She had to look at the numbers every single time.

She carried the big white carton to the counter. The total came to $3.71 with tax, and the man counted her change into her palm: six dollars and twenty-nine cents. She counted it again on the walk back, one coin at a time, and it matched. At the laundromat door she held up the carton like a trophy.

"I got the big one," she said. "It was cheaper per litre." Her mother raised an eyebrow at the change, counted it, and smiled. "Next time," she said, "check whether the orange juice follows the same rule."

The rain drove everyone into the craft cabin, and Payton's cabin had claimed the only table with the Monopoly box before Cabin 4 even finished tramping inside. Marcus from Cabin 4 wanted to play too, and after some arguing they agreed he could join, but only if he was the top hat, because nobody else wanted the top hat.

By the third lap around the board, trouble started. Marcus landed on Marvin Gardens and shook his head. "Too expensive. I'm saving for the railroads." He slid his token forward, but Payton put her hand flat on the board. "Wait. Nobody owns it. What happens now?" Devon shrugged. "Nothing happens. He skipped it." Payton frowned. She had a feeling, the same feeling she got in math class when an answer was too easy, that something hidden was going on, a rule nobody had ever read. She dug into the box and pulled out the folded rule sheet.

"There," she said, running her finger down the tiny print. "The official Monopoly rules say that if a player lands on an unowned property and chooses not to buy it, the bank auctions it to the players." Marcus groaned. "So I don't get to just pass it by?" "Nobody gets to just pass it by," Payton said, already sliding her chair forward. "Let's simulate it. Devon, you're the bank. Auction it off." Devon cleared his throat like a fancy auctioneer, which was so terrible it made everybody laugh, and Marvin Gardens went to Payton for a hundred and ten dollars because she was the only one who had read the whole rule.

Marcus bounced back fast, though. "Fine, but you're all being warned. I'm going to be the most versatile player this camp has ever seen. Railroads, utilities, whatever it takes." Nia pointed at his neat row of nothing. "Right now you're more like an herbivore. You only nibble the safe stuff." Marcus threw a plastic hotel at her, missed, and hit the top hat off the board. "Auction that," he said.

The gas station on Miller Road had two pumps, a rack of sun-faded maps, and a farm stand tucked beside the ice freezer where Mr. Ruiz sold peaches, corn, and whatever berries his cousin's farm sent over. Brooklyn sat on the curb while her dad tried to regulate the air pressure gauge, letting air out of the van's tires bit by bit until the numbers matched. She had eleven dollars in her pocket from walking Mrs. Chen's dog, and she had been planning for weeks to buy strawberries and make the fruit-and-yogurt cuisine from the cooking show she watched on Saturdays. The only problem was the price. Last month the little baskets had cost six dollars each, and she needed two.

A truck pulled in, and a woman in a paint-spattered shirt climbed out and headed straight for the stand. "Are these the last of the season?" she asked Mr. Ruiz, and Brooklyn's heart dropped. Last meant gone, and gone meant no smoothies. But Mr. Ruiz laughed. "Last? We're drowning in them. Peak of the local harvest came in this week, and the farmers have more than they know what to do with." He held up a basket. "Two fifty."

Brooklyn stood up so fast she knocked her dad's gauge against the tire. Two fifty? A month ago the same basket had been six dollars, because she had counted her money right there in that same spot and walked away with nothing. She thought about it while the woman bought four baskets, saying she wanted to paint the farmers' fields before summer ended. More berries than the farmers knew what to do with. That was the difference. When there had been only a few baskets, the price had been high; now that the trucks arrived full, the price had come down. She tested the idea in her head, turning it over like a coin. If she came back next week, even deeper into harvest, would they be cheaper still?

She walked to the stand and set her money on the counter. "Three baskets, please," she said, "and one for the lady with the paint, if she wants another." The woman turned around and smiled. "For my sister," she said. "She lives where the soil isn't half this fertile, and she misses real strawberries."

Aurora slid into the back seat holding the white envelope from the eye doctor's office, while Dad pulled out of the parking lot and the world outside revolved past the windows in slow loops of trees and parked cars. The glasses themselves wouldn't be ready for a week, but the paper inside the envelope was ready now, and she unfolded it on her knee. At the top it said her name, and beside her name, in small neat print, it said -2.00.

"Two negative," she said out loud, before she could stop herself.

"Two negative what?" Dad asked, checking the mirror and then the road.

"Two negative eyes, apparently." She turned the paper toward the window, as if brighter light might make the number friendlier. "I got a minus score. On my eyes." She had studied hard for the eye exam, or that was how she thought of it, reading every letter she could possibly read and guessing politely at the rest. Somewhere between the E and the fuzzy fourth line, something had gone wrong, and now the office had sent her a grade below zero.

Dad said the number was probably fine, but he said it the way people say things when they don't know either, so Aurora decided not to revolve the whole ride around his opinion. Instead she picked up the pamphlet the assistant had tucked into the envelope, the one about choosing frames. It had pictures of glasses with names like The Scholar and The Explorer, and a paragraph claiming the office had won some prestigious award for lens crafting, whatever that meant. Then, at the very back, she found a small chart. It showed the numbers from the prescription paper, and next to them two columns of words. The minus column said nearsighted. The plus column said farsighted. She read the top line twice. "Lens strength is measured in diopters," she said slowly, tasting the words. So the number measured the lenses, not her. And the minus wasn't a grade at all; it was a direction, and the opposite direction got a plus.

She wanted to be sure, so she tested it the only way she could without glasses. "Dad, what's a plus number mean?"

"Your mom's prescription is plus," he said. "She can't read a menu up close. Reads street signs fine from a mile away."

Aurora looked at the paper again. Minus two, nearsighted, and it was true, street signs blurred long before Dad said they should. The chart's logic held, and she had checked it against a real case. She folded the paper carefully and put it back in the envelope, then leaned her forehead against the cool window. The world outside was still soft at the edges, but only for one more week.

"One week," she said to her reflection in the glass. "Then I get my two whole diopters back."

The bus smelled like wet jackets, which was normal for a Tuesday in November. Gabrielle had just gotten comfortable against the window when DeShaun, two seats back, announced to the whole bus that the mayor was planning to tear down the ice rink and sell the land to a company that made foam fingers.

"That's a lie," said Priya, who lived near the rink and skated there every Saturday. "My mom would know."

"It was in a TV ad," DeShaun said. "I saw it with my own eyes. Twice."

Gabrielle turned around. She had opinions about the ice rink, mostly that the hot chocolate was overpriced, but an opinion and a thing somebody saw in an ad were not the same animal. She knew that much from dinner last spring, when her grandfather had repeated a claim from a commercial and her mother had looked it up on a website called PolitiFact. Founded in 2007, it rated claims on a scale called the Truth-O-Meter, from True all the way to something called Pants on Fire. Her grandfather had lost the argument, and also his dessert, though the two events were probably unrelated.

"An ad isn't proof," Gabrielle said. "It's just somebody's opinion wearing a suit."

DeShaun scoffed so hard he nearly inhaled his own gum. "Fine. Look it up, then."

Priya already had her phone out, but she couldn't use it, because she was on restriction until her mother picked up her new glasses prescription after school, and her mother checked the screen time like a hawk checks a field mouse. That left Gabrielle, who had exactly four percent battery and no desire to spend it on foam fingers.

The bus rattled past the retention pond, where a wedge of migratory geese stood around on the mud like they were waiting for a bus of their own. Gabrielle watched them and thought. DeShaun hadn't quoted the ad. He had paraphrased it, and people got things wrong when they paraphrased, especially people who half-watched TV while eating cereal. She'd done it herself last month, telling everyone the science teacher had canceled the field trip when Ms. Okafor had only postponed it.

"DeShaun," she said, "what did the ad actually say? Word for word."

He frowned. "Something about the mayor and the rink and jobs."

"Something about," Gabrielle repeated. "You paraphrased it. That's not the same as the ad being true, and it's not even the same as the ad saying what you said."

Priya leaned across the aisle, glasses prescription apparently forgotten, and read her mother's texts over her own shoulder, which took real talent. "My mom's group chat says the ad is about the mayor's vote on parking meters. The rink isn't mentioned."

Gabrielle's phone died at that exact moment, which she felt was dramatic but unhelpful. She turned around anyway. "Tonight I'll look it up on PolitiFact. They rate claims on a thing called the Truth-O-Meter, from True to Pants on Fire."

"Pants on Fire?" said DeShaun.

"That's what it's called," Gabrielle said. "My grandpa lost dessert to it."

Priya spent the rest of the ride planning a save-the-parking-meters campaign, just in case, and DeShaun spent it insisting he had still seen the ad twice. The geese, as far as anyone could tell, had no opinion at all.

Nathan had plans for this snow day, and they did not involve shoveling Mrs. Petra's driveway. He knocked on her door only because his mom had emphasized, three times, that neighbors help neighbors. "Two hands are better than one," Mrs. Petra said, handing him a second shovel, and Nathan felt a small bloom of resentment as her grandson Milo, age ten and full of energy, charged outside beside him.

Halfway down the driveway, Nathan stopped. He was staring at a chunk of ice he'd chipped from the steps, holding it up like evidence. "This is clear," he said. "Look straight through it. So how did a clear yard become a white one?" Milo scooped a snowball and shrugged. "It just is." Nathan didn't accept that. "Clear ice, white snow. Same stuff. Something happens when there's a lot of it."

He had an idea, and ideas made him move fast. He ran to the porch, grabbed the icicle hanging from the gutter, and carried it back like a sword. "Watch," he said. He smashed it against the driveway until it shattered into tiny glittering bits, then swept them into a pile with his mitten. Milo leaned in. The pile was white, unmistakably white, though every piece still flashed clear when Nathan held one up to the sun. "So the little pieces catch the light and throw it everywhere," Milo said slowly. "All the colors, every direction. That's why it looks white." Nathan pointed at the icicle's broken edge. "Billions of clear crystals doing that at once. A whole yard of it."

Mrs. Petra came out with cocoa, wiping her boots on the mat with its faded FLAMMABLE KEEP AWAY FROM HEATER sign, which she had propped hopefully by the firewood. She looked at the white pile of smashed ice and laughed. "You two solved winter in my driveway." Nathan took the cocoa, still buzzing, and eyed the untouched half of the driveway. "Race you to the sidewalk," Milo shouted, and Nathan threw down his cup and ran.

Zoe had agreed to keep Shabbat with her grandmother from Friday sundown until Saturday night, which meant no phone, no screens, no writing, for a whole day and part of another. She figured she could integrate one quiet afternoon into her life without much trouble, but by Saturday at four she was pacing the kitchen while her grandmother sliced apples for a cake nobody needed.

"Sit," her grandmother said. "The day ends when the sky says so, not when you do."

"How does the sky say so?" Zoe asked.

"Three stars. When you can see three stars, we say Havdalah. Havdalah means separation. It separates Shabbat from the rest of the week." Her grandmother slid the knife into the drawer. "Your mother and her brothers used to race to the window, all three of them, fighting over who counted first."

Zoe went to the front window anyway, mostly because the kitchen smelled like cinnamon and she had nothing else to do. Her cousin Theo, who was seven and lived next door, was already pressed against the glass. "I see one," he announced. "It's a star."

"It's a plane," Zoe said. "It's moving." She watched it slide sideways and blink out of sight, and she thought about that. If she counted moving lights, she'd end the day too early, and it wouldn't count. The rule, whatever principle was behind it, needed actual stars, and stars held still. So she made a plan: she would watch until each light had stayed put for a whole slow count of ten before she called it a star.

While they waited, Theo dug a folded paper out of the drawer under the phone, an old wooden thing Zoe had never seen anyone use. "Grandma said don't open it till after," he said, "but I can look at the outside." The paper was translucent where it had worn thin, and through it Zoe could make out the shape of handwriting on the other side. Her grandmother's, but older, with the letters pushed hard into the page. It was addressed to her mother, dated the summer her mother turned twelve. Zoe put it back in the drawer, unopened, because a promise was a promise even when nobody watched.

The sky went from gray to deep blue, and Theo bounced on the windowsill. Zoe counted her slow tens at each point of light. One star. Ten. Two stars. Ten. Then a third, small and steady above the neighbor's chimney. "Three," she said, and Theo yelled it toward the kitchen, and her grandmother came in with a braided candle, a small dish of spices, and a cup of wine.

But as her grandmother lit the candle, Zoe leaned close to the glass and checked her third star one more time. It had drifted. An airplane after all, creeping east. "Wait," she said. "That one's moving. I only have two."

Her grandmother cupped her hand around the flame. "So we wait," she said, and stood there in the doorway, patient as furniture. Zoe realized she had been hoping to catch her grandmother out, to prove the whole day was just rules somebody made up, and instead she had just caught a plane. A few minutes later a true star appeared beside the other two, holding its place through her count of ten, and this time she was sure.

They said Havdalah over the flame, and Theo tipped the cup so the wine ran out onto the dish, and Zoe smelled the spices and watched her grandmother's face flicker in the candlelight. Afterward she opened the drawer. The letter, it turned out, was one her mother had written to her grandmother that long-ago summer, saved and returned to the house by mail years later, asking to come home from camp because she missed Shabbat. Zoe read it twice, then texted her mother a photo of the window and the three dark patches of sky where the stars had been.

Zachary's mother worked the counter at First Savings on Saturdays, and he was allowed to sit in the back with a stack of brochures as long as he stayed out of the way. He was folding a brochure into a paper airplane when the edge of the paper sliced across his thumb, thin and quick, and a bead of red welled up like a tiny button. He blinked at it. How could something as floppy as paper do that? It was like being beaten up by a cloud.

"Paper cut," said Ms. Alvarez, the teller on window two, without even looking up. She slid a white first-aid box across the floor to him with her foot. "Corner of the paper. It's all edge, no face."

Zachary opened the box and found gauze, tape, three sizes of bandage, and a brown bottle labeled hydrogen peroxide. He knew that bottle. It fizzed white and bubbly on cuts, like a science experiment, and he'd always assumed the fizz meant it was working. He unscrewed the cap, but a laminated card was tucked under the bandages, and he paused to read it. Clean the wound with mild soap and water, the card said. Do not clean a cut with hydrogen peroxide or iodine, because both can irritate the wound. He read the line twice. "Huh," he said out loud. "The fizzing stuff is the wrong stuff."

"You learn something new every day," Ms. Alvarez said. A man at her window was arguing about a fee, so she lowered her voice. "My nephew soaked a scrape in peroxide last month. It stayed angry-looking for two weeks."

So Zachary tested it, in his own small way. He washed the cut under the break-room tap with soap and water, pressed the edges together, and peeled a bandage from its wrapper. He angled it so the pad covered the cut exactly, then smoothed the sticky wings down. The whole thing took less than a minute, and nothing fizzed at all. He tried to replicate the wrap on his other thumb with a second bandage, just to practice, and laughed when he got it crooked. "That one's for my left hand," he announced. "Left hand, crooked standard."

The card had one more part, a short list, and he read it under his breath: if the wound is deep, has ragged edges, or won't stop bleeding, see a doctor. His cut was shallow and clean-edged, and it had already stopped. He held his thumb up to the light like a jeweler inspecting a gem. "You pass," he told it.

On the way out, he passed a poster about mosquitoes, left over from some summer campaign, with the word parasite printed in bold across a cartoon bug. "Hey," he said to Ms. Alvarez, tapping the poster, "which is worse, a parasite, or a paper cut from a savings brochure?" She counted out twenties for her customer and kept a straight face. "At work, kid, everything's toxic to morale." Zachary grinned, pocketed two bandages for his backpack, and pushed through the heavy glass door with his uninjured hand.

The nurse's office smelled like Band-Aids and orange juice, and Rebecca could not stop bouncing her sneakers against the chair leg. Two weeks ago she had squinted at the whiteboard and copied a whole math problem wrong, and today, finally, there was a purple case waiting on the counter with her name on a sticker.

"New frames," said Nurse Okafor, sliding them across. "Go on."

Rebecca put them on. The eye chart across the room snapped into focus, but when she pulled her library book from her backpack, something even better happened. The tiny print, the print she'd been holding at arm's length all semester, went sharp as a blade. "Whoa," she whispered. "I can see the words."

Priya, sitting on the cot with an ice pack on her twisted ankle, laughed. "Congratulations, you're official." Then Priya squinted at her. "Wait. Your eyes look huge in those. Like, giant."

Rebecca leaned toward the mirror by the sink. It was true. Behind the new lenses her eyes looked swollen, like a cartoon character's. She frowned. Priya wore glasses too, and Priya's eyes always looked small, almost shrunken. Why would glasses puff one person's eyes up and squeeze another's down?

She had a theory. "Priya, let me try yours."

"Fine, but bring them back before the bell." Priya's ice pack wobbled as she handed them over. "I have that scholarship interview after school, and I want to actually see the interviewer."

Rebecca held Priya's glasses up to her library book. The page went into a blur. Then she looked through her own new lenses at the far wall, and the eye chart smudged. The two pairs did opposite jobs, so the lenses themselves had to be opposite, one kind bulging out and magnifying her eyes, one kind caving in and shrinking Priya's. She flipped the paper sleeve from her case and read the tag aloud: "Convex lenses."

"That's what yours are," Priya said. "Mine are the other kind. You're farsighted, like my grandpa. Light focuses behind your retina, so close stuff is blurry, and those fat lenses bend it back. I'm the reverse."

Rebecca held her glasses at arm's length and looked at Priya through them. Priya's ice pack, Priya's whole face, swelled magnified and strange, and Rebecca burst out laughing.

"I'm getting my picture taken for the yearbook on Friday," Priya groaned. "I'm going to look like a raisin."

"Or," Rebecca said, spinning the purple case in her hand, "you could borrow mine. The principal just appointed me to take the team photos for the announcement board, you know, and behind these lenses, everyone looks enormous."

Priya threw a pillow at her, and it sailed wide, blurred, and thumped onto the cot.

Scarlett had spent all of Tuesday's canoe class proving she was competent with a paddle, so on Wednesday the counselor, Ren, put her in charge of the new girl, Priya, who wanted more than anything to win Friday's talent show with her poem. Priya practiced constantly, whispering lines to herself by the lake. But at lunch Scarlett noticed something odd.
