I am staying on to the valley, for I came for land, not for gold." Colton had assumed everyone in these wagons wanted the same thing, but the diary was splitting them apart right in front of him. Some travelers came for farmland, and some came for money, pulled west by a discovery made before they even left home.

He filled two lines on his worksheet, then paused. One more page remained, and the ink there looked darker, newer. "October. A letter found me at last. Josiah writes from the mill. He has found little gold, but he has work weighing sacks for the miners, and he says the ground hums like a beehive. He asks me to save him a plot of land beside mine." Colton read it twice. The brother who had bolted for riches was now asking for exactly what Emmett had wanted all along.

Dana pointed at the final line of the diary. "Does it say what Emmett answered?"

Colton leaned closer. The last entry, dated a week later, read: "I have driven the fence posts to mark his half. He is my brother, and the valley has room."

"He saved it," Colton said quietly, still staring at the fence posts he would never see.

Nicolas skidded to a stop in front of the Rolling Race exhibit, where a long ramp curved down into a timing track. A basket of balls sat beside it, and a sign said: Measure distance. Measure time. Graph it. He grabbed a stopwatch from the bin, plucked out a bright orange ball, and turned to the kid already standing there, a girl with a clipboard and a pencil behind her ear.

"I bet my ball rolls faster than a person walks," Nicolas said. "Fast walking is about six kilometers per hour."

"Then you'd better measure," said the girl, whose name turned out to be Priya. She pointed to the marks on the track. "Every stripe is half a meter, and the counter shows seconds." They set the orange ball at the top of the ramp, and Priya counted down. "Three, two, one, go." The ball zipped down and crossed the three meter mark while the stopwatch read 1.4 seconds. Nicolas wrote the numbers on the back of his hand, then ran it again, because one try could be a fluke, and again. Three meters, always close to 1.4 seconds.

He worked the division on the edge of Priya's clipboard. "Three divided by 1.4 is about 2.1 meters per second. But walking speed is in kilometers per hour, not meters per second. How do you compare those?"

Priya tapped the panel on the exhibit wall, and there it was, printed under the title The Conversion Principle: to change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, multiply it by 3.6. Nicolas read it twice, then multiplied. "2.1 times 3.6 is about 7.6 kilometers per hour!" He leapt sideways out of the way of a toddler chasing a big buoyant foam ball that had bounced off the ramp. "Priya. PRIYA. That beats fast walking."

"It does," Priya said, already ruling lines on graph paper. "Now draw it. Distance on this side, time along the bottom." Nicolas plotted the three runs, and the dots climbed in a straight, stubborn line. "It's straight," he said. "Same slope every time. The ball doesn't slow down on the flat track, so the speed stays the same, and same speed means a straight line." Priya added one more point from a slow, heavy rubber ball she rolled herself, and its line lay flatter, like a hill tilted gently down.

"Yours is steeper," she said. "Steep line, fast ball." Nicolas stared at the two lines crossing his graph like roads, then flipped his stopwatch over and over in his hand. "Okay. New goal. Seven point six is good, but a sprinter does twenty kilometers per hour." He sprinted to the basket, dug all the way to the bottom, and came up holding a dense steel ball bearing. "You time," he said, already climbing to the top of the ramp.

Tyler sat near the window with the box in his backpack, and every time the bus bounced over a pothole he checked that the box was still there. His parents had finally decided to permit him a phone of his own, but only after he signed a list of rules on the fridge, all eleven of them. Rule six said the phone came to school but stayed in the backpack during class. Rule nine said he had to answer when his mom called. He had read the list three times at the kitchen table while his grandfather laughed and picked up the little phone, weighing it in one hand.

"Light as a biscuit," Grandpa said. "The first handheld cell phone call ever made, the man who made it, Martin Cooper, that phone weighed about one point one kilograms. Two and a half pounds." He handed it back to Tyler. "A kilogram and a bit. Like carrying a bag of sugar."

Tyler hadn't believed it at first. He had held the new phone in one palm and thought about the bag of sugar in the pantry, which was one kilogram, and his grandfather's number had to be right on top of that. Now, on the bus, he wanted to test it. In his backpack he had his history textbook, which the librarian had told him weighed one kilogram, because students always asked. He slid the book out, balanced the phone on top of it, and lifted both together. His hand dropped a little under the book alone. The phone was almost nothing.

"Are you weighing your phone with a textbook?" said Desmond, dropping into the seat across the aisle. Desmond was notorious for noticing everything, which was sometimes fun and sometimes not.

"Sort of an experiment," Tyler said. "My grandpa says the first handheld cell phone, the one Martin Cooper used for the first call, weighed about one point one kilograms. Two and a half pounds. Mine is way lighter than the book, and the book is one kilogram." He stacked them again, then held the book low and the phone high. "See? There's no comparison."

Desmond squinted at the little tower of phone and book. "So the first one weighed like a whole textbook plus some?"

"About that."

"That would wreck your pocket," Desmond said, and Tyler laughed and put the book away. Outside the window the fence posts went by in an even rhythm, and he felt the phone's thin weight through the canvas of the backpack, still exactly where he'd left it.

At his stop he climbed down the steps and patted the side pocket once. "Two and a half pounds," he said to himself, and walked up the drive.

Eli typed the last line of his program into the laptop and hit run. On the screen, a prompt blinked: ENTER A NUMBER. He typed 7, and the program printed PRIME. He typed 9, and it printed NOT PRIME. Behind him, Priya leaned over his shoulder, chewing the end of her pen. She had started the coding club's project board, and she wanted every program finished before Friday so the club could vote on which one to demo at the school assembly. "Try one," she said, so he typed 2. PRIME. Then 15. NOT PRIME.

"Try one," Priya said again, and this time she meant the actual number 1. Eli typed it. The screen said PRIME. He frowned at it. One felt like it should be prime. It wasn't even, and nothing divided it except one and itself, which happened to be the same thing. Priya tapped the screen. "That's wrong," she said. "One is not a prime number." She said it the way she said everything, flat and certain, and then she waited, because she wanted him to figure out the rest himself, or at least to try.

Eli could not see why. The rule he had coded, check every possible divisor, worked for 7 and 9 and 15, so the problem was not in the loops. It was in the rule itself, or in the number. He pulled a piece of scrap paper and wrote out products of primes. Six is two times three. Twelve is two times two times three. Fifteen is three times five. Each number came out one way, the same way every time he rewrote it. Then he tried one. One times one times one times one, on and on, and it never stopped. He sat back.

"Mathematicians exclude it," he said slowly, "so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes." Priya nodded. "That's the line for the board." The whiteboard in the computer lab held the club's rules, and next to it a ballot box made from a shoebox, where members dropped slips voting on the demo program. So far Eli's program had two votes and Marcus's maze game had four.

He added two lines to his code: if the number is one, print NOT PRIME. The school's filter sometimes blocked programs with certain words, but his complied with every rule, so it ran clean. Marcus came by and tested it twice, trying to break it, and the program sat there immune to every trick, printing NOT PRIME for 1 and 0, and PRIME for 13. Eli wrote his program's name on a slip, folded it, and dropped it in the ballot box. "Vote for yourself?" Priya said. "Vote for the math," said Eli, and closed the lid.

The basketball court behind the middle school had been chalked off into a rough oval that spring, because Coach Reyes liked his runners to practice somewhere with fences and cracks and obstacles, something a smooth track never offered. Ethan stood at the painted start line with six other boys, and Coach walked the curve with a clipboard, taking a quick census of who was racing the eight hundred and who had signed up for the sprints. Ethan raised his hand.

"The eight hundred is exactly two laps," Coach said, tapping the chalk oval. "On a four-hundred-metre track, two laps, that's the whole race. First lap, second lap. Nothing else." Then he blew the whistle before anyone could ask more.

Ethan had a plan, and the plan was simple: hold back on the first lap so his legs still worked on the second. The trouble was the boy next to him, a tall kid named Marcus from another school who wore mismatched shoes and ran with a flailing, eccentric arm swing that made him look like he was swatting bees. Marcus shot off the line like the race was twenty metres long. Ethan let him go, counting his own strides, keeping something in the tank, the way he'd practiced.

At the end of the first lap, Marcus sprinted. He surged past the chalk line, arms wide, grinning at the fence where the spectators stood, and slowed to a walk with his hands on his head, victorious. Nobody moved. The boy in third place glanced at Coach, confused. Marcus turned around, still breathing hard, and his grin faded.

Ethan passed him, and while he passed him he understood. Marcus hadn't run two laps. He had run one. He'd kicked for the finish a full lap too early, because he'd lost count, and an eight hundred wasn't over at the line, it was only half over. That was the hidden rule of the race, invisible on the chalk, and Ethan could deduce it from Marcus's face alone: the slow dawning horror of a boy doing the math.

The second lap hurt. Ethan's legs burned and his arms pumped and the bee-swatting kid behind him started running again, furious now, closing the gap stride by stride. The fence came up fast. Ethan leaned, drove his knees, crossed the chalk a second time and stumbled onto the grass, gasping.

Marcus finished three seconds later and stood over him, shaking his head. "Two laps," he said. "Nobody told me it was two laps."

"Everybody told you," Ethan wheezed. "You just ran the wrong half first."

Grandpa's den smelled like pencil shavings and coffee, and the old laptop on his desk made a soft humming sound as Payton typed. She had wanted to build something real all summer, not just play games, and yesterday Grandpa had challenged her: write a program that asks for a number and tells you whether it is prime. "A prime number," he had said, "is only divisible by 1 and itself." That part she understood. The hard part was teaching the computer to check.

Her first idea was simple. Take the number, try dividing it by every smaller number, and if any division came out even, the number was not prime. She wrote a loop with a variable called divisor, ran the program, and typed in 15. "Not prime," the screen said. She punched the air. Then she tried 9, then 25, then 13. All correct. She was feeling like a diplomat negotiating a peace treaty between herself and the machine, and winning.

Then she typed 2.

"Not prime," the screen said.

Payton stared at it. That was wrong. She knew 2 was prime; she had known that since fourth grade. So where was the mistake hiding? She couldn't see it, because the loop was invisible once it ran. All she could see was the answer. She rested her chin on her hand and traced the code with her finger, line by line. "Divide the number by every smaller number," she whispered. Smaller than 2. There was nothing smaller than 2 to divide by, except 1, and dividing by 1 never counted. She exhaled slowly, fogging the corner of the screen. The loop never found anything, so her program reported... not prime? No, wait. If nothing divided evenly, it should say prime. Unless her code had the conditions backwards.

She looked again at her if statement and found it: she had written the print lines in the wrong order, so a number with no divisors got labeled "not prime." That meant every prime would fail, not just 2. She fixed the swap and ran it again. 13: prime. 2: prime. Then she tried 4, and the screen said "Not prime," which was right, because 4 could be divided evenly by 2. So could 6, and 8, and 10, she realized. Two was the only even prime number, the only one standing alone.

The mistakes were starting to feel cumulative, one stacking on another, but so were the fixes. Grandpa appeared in the doorway with two mugs of cocoa. "So?" he asked.

Payton typed 2 one more time and turned the screen toward him. "Prime," it said.

Annabelle crouched at the top of the skate park's smallest ramp with a stopwatch in one hand and a tennis ball in the other. Her science project was due tomorrow morning, and she still needed a graph of the ball's speed. Down at the bottom of the ramp, her friend Dez held a tape measure stretched along the smooth concrete, drumming his fingers on his knee. "Can we hurry?" he said. "I signed up for the beginners' trick clinic at four, and if I miss it, I lose my spot."

"Ten more minutes," Annabelle said. "I promise." She had marked the ramp every meter with chalk, and her plan was simple: roll the ball, time it, write down where it was at each second. But she didn't just want numbers. She wanted to know what the ball's motion looked like, and you couldn't see speed itself, only see where the ball was and when. She wondered what shape all those little measurements would make if she connected them.

She rolled the ball and clicked the stopwatch, calling out positions as it passed each chalk mark. They ran three trials, then sat on the edge of the half-pipe and plotted the points on graph paper. Annabelle drew the axis for distance and the axis for time, then connected the dots. She sat back. "Look at this. It's almost perfectly straight." The line climbed steadily up the page, like a ramp drawn in ink. Was that normal, or had they measured wrong? She had expected some wobbly curve, something messy, because the ball was speeding along and then slowing and she couldn't watch it closely.

Dez leaned over her shoulder, but his eyes kept drifting to the older skaters carving the big bowl. "Is that bad?" he asked. Annabelle shook her head slowly. "No. A straight sloping line means it's going at a constant speed." She tried it in her head. The ball on the smooth concrete covered the same distance every second, so every point sat evenly along one line. She rolled the ball again on the rough gravel by the fence, plotted those points, and got a line that bent and flattened. The concrete ramp made the straight line; the gravel did not.

"See? Same ball, different surface, different shape," she said, tapping the two graphs side by side. "Mr. Okafor will ask me how I know it's constant speed, and now I can justify my answer with both graphs, not just a guess." Dez stood up and grabbed his board. "Good, because I have to justify skipping my clinic to my grandpa, and he already thinks skateboarding will bankrupt his pension if I break another helmet." Annabelle laughed and packed her papers into her backpack.

At the gate she paused, looking back at the empty ramp, already wondering whether the ball would make a straighter line on the bigger ramp, or whether a steeper line meant a faster ball. "Tomorrow after school," she said to Dez, "want to help me with one more trial?" Dez balanced his board on one hand and grinned. "Only if I get to roll it off the tall ramp first."

On Saturday morning Lucy stood in her kitchen, staring at the permission slip her mom had signed the night before. It said she would volunteer at the community food bank from nine until noon, and the words alone were enough to intimidate her. She had never been, and she pictured a giant warehouse full of strangers who all knew exactly what to do except her.

"Take the muffins," her mom said, sliding a paper bag across the counter. "Ask for Mr. Okafor. And Lucy, if the neighbor's cat comes near the birds again, shoo him off, okay? That animal is pure predatory instinct in a fur coat."

The cat was already crouched under the feeder, tail twitching, eyes fixed on the sparrows. Lucy banged the door on her way out and he fled, offended.

The food bank turned out to be smaller than she'd imagined, more like a big garage than a warehouse, with shelves of canned beans and rice rising to the ceiling. Mr. Okafor handed her a clipboard. "You're on inventory. Count the pasta, write the number, don't guess."

A boy about her age, Deshawn, was already at the next shelf, counting fast. "I'm here every weekend," he said. "My grandma used to come here for groceries. Now I want to work here someday, for real. Paycheck and everything."

Mid-morning, a truck backed up to the loading door, and Lucy noticed a logo on its side, a bowl with a fork. "That's the second truck today with that same picture," she said. "But the first one had Dallas plates and this one's local. How can they both have it?"

Deshawn shrugged. Mr. Okafor kept unloading. Lucy chewed her pencil. Same logo, different cities. It couldn't be a coincidence, and it couldn't be that one company owned trucks everywhere. Her guess: it had to be some kind of network, one name covering lots of separate food banks.

She found the answer on a poster by the office door. "Feeding America," she read slowly. "It's a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks." She counted the words twice. More than two hundred. Dallas, her town, and probably everywhere else.

"So we're connected to Dallas," she told Deshawn.

"That's why the trucks look alike," he said. "Huh. Whole country's in on it." He went back to counting, but he was grinning.

At noon, Lucy carried out the empty muffin bag and found the neighbor's cat back under the feeder, frozen like a statue. The sparrows' calm was an illusion; they hadn't seen him yet. She clapped her hands and they scattered upward, safe.

"See you next Saturday," Deshawn called from the door. Lucy waved and walked home, already planning to sign up again.

Eleanor pulled the tray of chicken out of the fridge and set it on the counter, right beside the cutting board she had just used to trim the raw meat. Outside the window the sky had turned an ominous gray, and rain streaked the glass, which meant her little brother would be trapped inside and cranky all evening. She had promised her parents a full dinner tonight, chicken and salad and rice, because Mom had to work late and Dad's bus ran slow on rainy days.

She rinsed the knife, dried it, and reached for the head of lettuce. Then she stopped, her hand hovering over the board. It looked clean enough, just a few faint streaks where the chicken had lain, but she remembered the health video from school and the word that had come with it. Something about invisible things traveling from one food to another. She couldn't see anything on the board, but that was exactly the problem. What you couldn't see could still be there.

"Cross-contamination," she said out loud, testing the word. Her brother, Sam, wandered in and stole a carrot from the bowl.

"Is that a band?"

"It's how bacteria spread from one food to another. Like from raw meat to stuff you eat raw, like salad." She slid the used board into the sink, ran hot water and soap over it, and pulled a clean board from the cabinet. She set the lettuce on the fresh plastic and started chopping, feeling a little smug about her own cleverness.

When Dad finally came in, shaking rain off his jacket, he found her arranging the salad and the chicken already browning in the pan. He peered over her shoulder at the two boards, one in the drying rack, one on the counter.

"Did you use separate boards for the chicken and the lettuce?" he asked.

"Of course," Eleanor said. "I'm not going to chop salad on the board that had raw chicken on it."

Dad smiled and began to elaborate on how proud he was, telling her about the time in college he'd made himself sick with a midnight sandwich, until Sam groaned and begged him to stop. While Dad set the table, the radio muttered about heavy precipitation moving in overnight, up to two inches, and possible flooding near the river.

"Great," Sam said. "Indoor recess forever."

"Then you're helping me make cookies tomorrow," Eleanor said. She tipped the salad into the good bowl, the one with the blue rim, and carried it to the table.

The pavilion at Riverside Park had been decorated since morning, and Gabriel arrived with his mother, his tía Rosa, and a plastic bag holding one sugar skull that had already lost an arm. A banner over the tables read "Día de los Muertos, November 1 and 2." His tía had explained in the car, more than once, that in Mexico these were the days for honoring family members who had died, and that families built altars in their homes for it. Gabriel mostly cared about one thing: he was supposed to add his grandfather's photo to the community altar today, and he had left the photo in the printer tray at home.

The altar stood at the end of the longest table. A girl from his class, Marisol, was arranging frames on it. "It's called an ofrenda," she said when he stood there too long without doing anything. "My great-grandfather goes here." She set down a photo of a man in a straw hat holding a radio.

Gabriel checked his mother's phone for the picture he wanted, the one of his grandfather laughing at a barbecue. The battery bar was red, then the screen went black. He borrowed Tía Rosa's phone, but the photo had never been sent to her. He had a copy only at home, and home was a twenty-minute walk.

While he decided what to do, he noticed something odd. The candles on the ofrenda kept going out. Marisol relit one, and it died again within a minute. An old man nearby blamed the candles themselves, saying they were cheap, but Gabriel crouched and watched. The flames all bent in the same direction, toward the lake. When a group of people walked past the open side of the pavilion, the flames accelerated sideways, flickered hard, and went out. It wasn't the candles. Wind was funneling between the two support posts on the north side, and the candles sat directly in that channel.

He tested it by holding a single candle near the posts, then behind the stacked pan de muerto at the center of the table. At the posts it guttered. Behind the bread, the flame stood still. He and Marisol moved the candleholders to the sheltered middle of the ofrenda, and none of them went out for the rest of the afternoon. The old man gave a small nod, as if he had suspected wind all along.

Then Gabriel ran home. He got the photo, ran back through the falling leaves, out of breath, and slid it into an empty frame Marisol had saved. He placed it beside her great-grandfather with the radio.

When his mother saw it, she said, "He would have liked being next to somebody who loved music that much."

Gabriel straightened the frame so his grandfather's grin faced the whole park.

Justin stood in line at Hartley's Pharmacy behind his mom, breathing through his mouth because his nose was still packed solid. Two days ago he'd been flattened by the flu, shivering under three blankets and watching the ceiling fan spin. Now his fever was gone and he mostly felt like a deflated soccer ball instead of a popped one, which to him meant one thing: he was better.

The party was the problem. Devon's birthday started at two o'clock, and there would be pizza, a game tournament, and a dog named Biscuit who did tricks for carrot sticks. Justin had RSVP'd weeks ago, back when the flu was just a rumor in the seventh-grade hallway. He held the pharmacy's number card, number 17, and rehearsed his argument while the fluorescent lights buzzed overhead and the smell of hand sanitizer drifted from the counter.

"Prescription for Mara Ellis," the pharmacist called, and Justin's mom stepped up. That gave Justin an idea. While she signed the pickup slip, he leaned toward the pharmacist, a woman with silver hoops and glasses on a beaded chain, and asked his question like a scientist gathering data. "If somebody had the flu and their fever's gone on day two, are they done being contagious? Hypothetically."

She smiled at "hypothetically." "Nice try. According to the CDC, people with the flu are most contagious during the first three days of their illness. Day two means you're right in the middle of the danger zone, hypothetical or not."

Justin did the math in his head, and the math was terrible. He was on day two. Three days of maximum contagion meant tomorrow and part of Sunday too. He tested a loophole anyway. "What if I just don't cough on anyone? What if I stand by the window?"

"Viruses thrive in exactly the conditions you can't control," the pharmacist said, dropping the white paper bag into his mom's hands. "Kids at a party, sharing controllers, passing pizza."

Walking to the car, Justin tried one last angle with his mom. "Is a partial appearance feasible? Like, ten minutes?"

"You mean is it feasible for you to give Devon the flu for his birthday?" she said, unlocking the doors. "No."

So Justin built a backup plan. He video-called Devon at two o'clock, propped his phone against the cereal box, and played the tournament remotely, shouting instructions while Devon's little sister acted as his hands on the controller. He was losing badly and laughing about it when a knock came at his own door and his mom appeared with a plate. Pizza, she said, from a delivery that had mysteriously been ordered to the wrong address, which happened to be theirs.

"Devon says hi," she said, and behind her, faintly, through the phone, Biscuit the dog barked.

Alexis stood in the laundry aisle of Hillcrest Grocery with a crumpled list in one hand and a grudge in the other. Last week her favorite hoodie had come out of the wash the size of a hamster sweater, and her mom had said, maybe next time you let me handle it. No. Alexis was going to handle it. She was going to become a fully competent laundry person, and the hoodie incident would be remembered as history.

"Detergent, stain spray, bleach," she read off the list. "For whites. And the ammonia spray for the bathroom, it's on sale." She grabbed a jug of chlorine bleach, then reached for the ammonia cleaner, planning to stack them in the cart like good friends.

Then she flipped the bottles over and read the backs, because her science teacher had made them do that once with a bottle of drain opener and it had been mildly terrifying. The bleach label said never mix with cleaners containing ammonia. The ammonia label said the same thing in bolder letters, like it was yelling in print. Together they release chloramine, a toxic gas.

Alexis held the two bottles at arm's length from each other, as if they might leap. "You two are not carpooling," she informed them. She set the bleach in the front of the cart and the ammonia spray way down in the back, under the paper towels, where they couldn't even see each other.

Her little brother Theo appeared around the end cap, drawn to her like a parasite that feeds on embarrassing moments. "Are you talking to cleaning supplies?"

"They emit poison gas if they mix," Alexis said. "Chloramine. I'm keeping them apart."

"Wow. A toxic friendship." Theo dropped a bag of gummy worms in the cart. "Anyway, Mom says hurry up, and also she says don't buy the pink-tinted detergent, whatever that means."

At home, Alexis carried out her plan with ceremony. She sorted the laundry into three piles on the living room floor: whites, darks, and a suspicious middle pile she labeled "???". She tested one mystery sock by dipping its corner in warm water and pressing it against an old white rag. No pink came off, so into the whites it went. Cold water, detergent, whites first. She even read the bleach cap to measure it properly, and she remembered the aisle and measured it over the sink, far from anything ammonia.

When she pulled the load out, every sock was still white, the towels smelled like clean rain, and she folded everything into a stack so neat it looked store-bought. She carried it upstairs like a trophy.

Her mom was standing in the doorway of the laundry room, holding the shrunken hoodie and grinning. "Want to know a secret? I didn't shrink your hoodie. It went in the dryer with Theo's wool hat. He sneaks it in because he thinks it softens his pillows."

From down the hall came Theo's voice: "It works, though!"

The clock above the whiteboard said twelve minutes left, and Maria still had no topic for the class discussion her grade depended on. Mr. Ruiz had given everyone until the end of the period to bring forward one real experiment and explain why it mattered. Around her, kids were scribbling last-minute notes about volcanoes and vinegar.

Then Marcus leaned across the aisle. "You were in the hallway yesterday when Devon and that seventh grader crashed, right? How fast were they going?"

"Fast," Maria said. "They smashed into each other. Twenty miles an hour, easy." She said it with certainty, and then a small cold feeling moved through her, because she realized she had only seen the last half second of it. The word smashed had come from her father, who had asked about the collision at breakfast. How fast were they going when they smashed into each other? That was what he'd said.

She raised her hand. "Mr. Ruiz, can I survey the class in the next ten minutes? For my experiment."

"Make it quick," he said, and shrugged as if he expected nothing.

Maria stood at the front with her notebook. Half the class had been in the hallway yesterday and half had only heard about it. She split them. To the window side she asked, "How fast were the two boys going when they hit each other?" To the door side she asked, "How fast were they going when they smashed into each other?" She kept her voice flat for both questions, like a scientist installing a sensor and walking away without touching it.

The door side shouted numbers at her. Twenty, twenty-five, one kid said thirty. The window side mumbled. Ten, maybe twelve. Nobody on that side went above fifteen. She wrote the two columns on the board, and the room went quiet in a way that felt almost sinister, everyone staring at the gap between them. Same collision, same boys, same tiled hallway. Two different sets of numbers.

"There was a real study," Marcus said suddenly, pulling out his phone. "My mom talks about it. 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer." He read slowly off the screen. "People who were asked how fast cars smashed into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that hit."

"Say that again," Maria said, and he did. She checked her columns against it and her neck went hot. The direction matched. Her question, her one changed word, had pushed the numbers up, exactly as it had pushed her own memory up at breakfast.

Mr. Ruiz checked the clock. "Two minutes. So what's your topic, Maria?"

"People don't just remember things," she said. "The question itself gets into the memory. I know because my dad asked me if those boys smashed, and I was sure it was twenty miles an hour until five minutes ago." She tapped the board. "Same hallway. Same crash. The word did that."

Marcus looked at her column, then at his own door-side estimate, and raised his hand to lower his number.

Nevaeh's brother Marcus had claimed the kitchen table for his audition, which meant he was filming himself doing a card trick with the family's only good lamp shining in his face. That left Nevaeh the counter by the toaster, where she set down the microscope she had borrowed from school, a plastic bag with an onion, and her lab sheet with three blank labels waiting: cell wall, membrane, nucleus.

Mr. Ruiz had let her take the microscope because Monday was the science fair and Saturday was the only day she had. If she couldn't get a slide focused tonight, she would have to draw her cells from the textbook, and everyone could tell a textbook drawing from a real one, because textbook cells were tidy and real ones never were.

She peeled a paper-thin layer of skin off the onion, laid it on the slide with a drop of water, and lowered the cover slip. Then she swung the biggest lens into place, the one marked 40x, because that one was obviously the best one. She pressed her eye to the eyepiece and saw a turbulent gray fog, like weather. She moved the slide left, then right. Fog. Up. Fog. She began to assume the onion had betrayed her, or the microscope was broken, or Mr. Ruiz had sent her home with a lemon on purpose.

Marcus leaned over her shoulder. "What's it supposed to be?"

"Onion cells. It's supposed to be onion cells."

"Looks like a screen door in a hurricane," he said, and went back to his cards.

She turned the focus knob slowly, one full turn, and nothing happened except the fog got denser. She lifted her head and glared at the three lenses on the rotating wheel, 4x, 10x, 40x, and thought about it. If the whole slide was a fog at 40x, maybe she was zoomed in too far to find anything. The field of view at the bottom would be tiny, like looking for a house through a keyhole. She swung the smallest lens, the 4x, into place.

Under the low power, the fog arranged itself into shapes. There they were, rows of cells like bricks in a wall, pale and slightly crooked. She centered them, turned the fine focus until the edges went crisp, then, carefully, swung the lens up to 10x. The cells stayed put, bigger now. She found the nucleus, a small dark dot in each cell, and the wall around every one of them. At 40x she could even make out the thin line of the membrane just inside the wall, which the diagram in her textbook had drawn too fat. She labeled all three and felt reasonably magnificent.

Marcus appeared behind her with his deck of cards. "Can I look?"

"You have an audition."

"The audition can wait." He shoved the deck in his pocket. "Show me the onion."

She swung the lens back down to the lowest power first, found the cells again, and stepped aside. "Okay. Now it's your turn to find one."

Luca carried four bean plants into the gymnasium, balancing the pots against his chest while his display board flapped in his other hand. Behind the folding table marked "Project 23," his heart was pounding. He had spent six weeks spraying three of the plants with different amounts of his homemade fertilizer, measuring their heights every single day, and his reputation as the kid who could actually finish what he started was on the line here.

The first judge, a woman with a clipboard, stopped at his table and tilted her head. "Interesting. Three plants, three fertilizer amounts. But which one would have grown like that anyway?" Luca opened his mouth and then closed it. He hadn't thought about that question at all. He looked at his data chart, the neat columns of numbers he was so proud of, and realized they showed nothing to compare against.

While the judge moved on, Luca sank onto a folding chair. His friend Priya leaned over from the next table, where her project on endangered wetland birds was spread out in a fan of photographs. "You look like your whole project just embarrassed you in public," she said. He explained the problem, and she squinted at his plants. "My cousin did a project like this. She kept one plant that got nothing new at all. Same sun, same water, just no fertilizer."

Luca stared at the fourth pot still sitting on his windowsill at home, the one he had grown but ignored because it got no treatment. "A control group," he said slowly. "It gets no change at all, so you can compare the tested plants against it." He grabbed his phone, texted his mom, and fifteen minutes later she walked in carrying the pot with a sheepish wave. Luca rearranged his table, putting the untreated plant right in the center, and added a new column to his chart in green marker: the heights of the plant that had grown on plain water alone.

When the judge came back around, Luca walked her through all four plants. "This one got no fertilizer," he said, tapping the center pot. "So the others are being compared against it, not just against each other." She made a note on her clipboard and gave him a small nod, the kind that meant something. Later, when Mr. Delgado announced the ribbon winners, Luca's name was third on the list for honorable mention. Priya squeezed his shoulder. "Next year," she said, "we start with the control group on day one." Luca grinned and slid the green marker back into his pocket.

The bleachers in the gym were packed, and Victor sat on the folding chair on stage with his number pinned to his shirt, trying not to tap his foot. He had made it to the final three, and the word that had just knocked out the girl beside him was "colleague." Victor would have missed it too, two weeks ago. Back then he had been furious about words like "bite" and "knife," where the e sat at the end saying nothing at all, and he'd been ready to postpone the whole bee and quit.

Then he found a dusty book in the school library, a frugal little paperback with a cracked spine, and everything changed. He read that between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift, and it happened after spellings had started to become fixed. That was why the letters stopped matching the sounds. Victor tested it on a napkin at lunch, listing "bite," "mate," "hope," and realizing the pattern ran through half his list. The letters weren't broken; they were holding still while the sounds moved underneath them, like a fence on a shifting frontier. His friend Deja had leaned over his shoulder in the cafeteria and said, "The Great Vowel Shift? Never heard of it," and he'd shown her the book.

Now the judge said, "Victor, your word is 'misled.'" Victor's first instinct was M-I-S-L-E-D, because that was how it looked on the page. But he paused. Under the old pattern, that e would have made the i long, and nobody said "mizzled." The spelling was a trap from the same old shift, a fossil of how things used to sound. He thought it through again. "M, I, S, L, E, D." The judge nodded, and Victor let out a breath.

Two rounds later, only he and a tall kid named Rashad were left. Rashad got "biscuit" and spelled it cleanly. Then it was Victor again. "Your word is 'conscientious.'" Victor closed his eyes for a second. He used to think spelling was just memorizing nonsense, that some words were simply unfair. Now he saw each weird letter as a clue, something left behind by sound that had drifted away centuries before anyone alive was born. The c before the t, the tricky ious ending; he walked through it piece by piece.

"C-O-N-S-C-I-E-N-T-I-O-U-S." The gym went quiet while the judge checked the card, and then her voice rang out across the basketball court: "That is correct."

Rashad grinned and shook Victor's hand. "Rematch next year," he said. "But you have to tell me where you learned all that."

Alyssa carried the crate into the kitchen the way her mother had carried her when she was little, slow and careful, like the thing inside might break. Inside was a small brown dog with floppy ears, adopted that morning from the shelter, and Alyssa had already decided his name was Biscuit. She set the crate down, opened the door, and waited while he crept out and sniffed the baseboards, the table leg, her sneaker.

"You're home now," she told him.

Her friend Marisol came over after lunch to see him, carrying a bag of trail mix. They took Biscuit out to the backyard, where he chased a fallen leaf in circles until he tripped over his own feet. Marisol laughed so hard she had to sit down on the porch step. When Biscuit trotted over and put his chin on her knee, she reached into the bag.

"No, wait," Alyssa said, grabbing her wrist. Something was nagging at her, a memory she couldn't quite pin down. "Hold on. I read something."

"About trail mix?"

"About one thing in it. Give me a second." She closed her eyes and tried to interpret the fuzzy memory, the way you might squint at a smudged whiteboard. She had been in the waiting room at the shelter, flipping through a pamphlet while her mom filled out paperwork. There had been a list. She remembered the word "never."

The flashback came clear: fluorescent lights, a plastic chair digging into her back, a page with a box drawn around it. Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, the box had said, so they should never be given as treats. She had skimmed it then, thinking it was boring fine print. Now it felt like she'd read a warning label after already lighting the match.

"Raisins," she said out loud. "They're in trail mix. Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, so they should never be given as treats. That was in the pamphlet."

Marisol looked at the bag. "It's just raisins, not grapes."

"It said both. Grapes and raisins." Alyssa picked up the bag, walked it inside, and came back with a jar of peanut butter and a spoon instead. Biscuit licked the spoon clean and then tried to eat the spoon.

The rest of the afternoon Alyssa watched him closely, wondering how a thing as small as a raisin could matter so much, and how many other invisible rules were out there waiting. What else could hurt him that she hadn't read about yet? She made a list on the fridge: peanut butter, yes; raisins, no; grapes, no. Then she added a question mark, because there had to be more.

That night she looked up dogs and chocolate too, and the answer made her glad Marisol hadn't brought brownies. Biscuit curled up on her bedroom floor, mostly asleep but twitching, his paws moving like he was running somewhere. Dogs aren't nocturnal, she thought, so why was he awake? She wrote that down as her next question. Then Biscuit sighed, rolled over, and slept.

Elliot had exactly one week to figure out the difference between simple and compound interest before the fifth-grade math fair, and his poster board sat blank on his desk like a desolate white tundra. His want was simple enough: the prize was a real twenty-five-dollar savings bond, and his older sister Dana had won it two years ago. If a Reyes sibling won twice in a row, their grandfather promised to frame both certificates side by side in the hallway. Elliot wanted that wall.

The teacher, Ms. Okafor, had given them each a pretend bank account with one hundred dollars. "Simple interest pays on the principal only," she said, and left it at that, because the whole point of the fair was that they figure out the rest themselves. That was the dilemma: Elliot could calculate simple interest easily, five percent of one hundred dollars every year for five years, but compound interest did something strange on his calculator. Each year the interest payment grew a little, even though he added nothing.

He asked his friend Ruby, who was building a volcano and had her own problem, since her baking soda had run out and the fair was Friday. "Can I borrow your math brain for five minutes if I let you use my poster paint?" she said. Elliot agreed, but Ruby only shrugged at the numbers. "Mine stays the same every year. Yours goes up. That's all I've got."

The answer came in an unexpected place. Dana had written him a note and slipped it into his backpack, since she was away at a track meet and couldn't help him in person. "Dear genius-in-training," the note read, "Grandpa took me to the bank yesterday and I watched them post my interest. It grew from last year even though I deposited nothing, and the teller smiled and said compound interest is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself starts earning interest. Thought that might matter to you. Don't spend my paint. Dana." Elliot read it three times under his desk, then went back to his calculator with his heart drumming. One hundred dollars, five percent, five years. Simple gave him twenty-five dollars of interest. Compound gave him a little over twenty-seven, and the extra came from the interest earning its own interest, exactly as Dana's note said.

He raised his hand to clarify one thing with Ms. Okafor, only whether he could show both columns side by side, and she nodded. After school, Ruby knocked on his door holding a new box of baking soda her dad had bought, and a jar of glitter paint for him anyway. They worked at his kitchen table until dark, her volcano bubbling in the sink, his poster filling with two climbing bars, one straight and one curving slowly upward.

At the fair on Friday, the judge stood at Elliot's table for a long time, tracing the two lines with her finger. "Which one would you want?" she asked.

Elliot pointed at the curve. "That one. The interest gets paid interest too."

Kaitlyn paced the empty front row of the auditorium, index cards snapping between her fingers. In three days she and Marcus would debate the school board's homework policy, and their first practice had been a disaster.

"You said homework is useless," Coach Rivera had told Marcus. "That's your claim. Now where's your evidence?" Marcus had just shrugged and said it louder, which was when Kaitlyn realized that volume was not the same thing as an argument.

Marcus arrived now with a binder and a bag of chips. "I presume you've got our case ready," he said, flopping into a seat.

"Half of it." Kaitlyn laid her cards on the stage. "Coach kept calling my points claims. The claim is the point being argued, right? Like, homework should be capped at thirty minutes a night. That's the claim. But a claim alone is just an opinion."

"So what's the rest?"

She flipped a card. "I looked it up last night. The evidence has a name too. In this argument model, the grounds, or data, are the evidence given to support the claim." She slid a printout toward him, a graph of student sleep hours. "So this is our grounds. Sixth graders with more than an hour of homework sleep forty minutes less."

Marcus squinted at it. "Okay, but a debate judge could still say, so what? Maybe they stay up playing games."

"Exactly. That's the part I couldn't figure out yesterday." Kaitlyn drew three boxes on a card and connected them with arrows. "You need the middle piece, the thing that ties the evidence to the claim. I tested it on my brother. I told him kids with heavy homework sleep less, and he said, 'Why should the school care?' So I added, if students are sleep-deprived, they learn worse, so the school's own goal is defeated. He actually nodded."

"That's the warrant," Marcus said, reading over her shoulder. "It's on the worksheet Coach gave us. You built it without knowing the word."

Kaitlyn laughed and started copying her boxes onto fresh cards, one for each point. Marcus pulled out his own stack of opinions and began hunting for grounds behind each one, crossing out two entirely.

"Let's run a hypothetical," he said, standing. "You're the judge, I'm the other team. I attack your sleep study."

Kaitlyn squared her cards, faced the empty seats, and said, "Ladies and gentlemen, our first claim."

The seatbelt dug into Maya's chest in a way it never used to, and she kept tugging at it while Dad drove toward the mall. Everything about her felt slightly rearranged lately, like someone had moved the furniture inside her body overnight. She was thirteen now, and Priya's birthday pool party was on Saturday, and Maya had one thing on her mind that she couldn't say out loud: she hadn't gotten her period yet, and it seemed like everyone at school already had.

"Dad, can we swing by Priya's house on the way?" she asked. "Just for ten minutes?"

Dad checked the mirror. "Your brother has soccer at four. You're cutting it close."

"Ten minutes," Maya said. "I'll time it myself."

In the back seat, her little brother Leo groaned. He wanted to stop at the game store to trade in two old cartridges, and their errands were already piling up while the afternoon dwindled away. "You always get your stops," he complained. "I never get mine."

"Because your stops involve forty minutes of arguing with the guy at the counter," Dad said, but he turned onto Priya's street anyway, which made Leo slump against the window in defeat.

Priya dragged Maya up to her room, where the walls were covered with posters and her two older sisters' old trophies still sat on the shelf. "You look like you're on a mission," Priya said.

"I have a question, and you're the only person I can ask." Maya sat on the bed. "Your sisters. Did they get their periods at the same age?"

Priya blinked, then grinned. "That's your mission? No. Nina was twelve, almost exactly. Dia was fourteen. My mom said the same thing happened with her and her sister." She pulled a folded printout from a drawer, some school project. "There's this big CDC survey, it found the median age is about twelve. But Dia still counts as normal, because there's a really wide normal range around it."

Maya stared at the number. Twelve. She'd been doing quiet math for weeks, assuming there was a deadline she'd already missed. But a median wasn't a deadline, was it? It was just a middle. Half before, half after, all of it normal. Her logic had been wrong from the start, and the wrongness felt wonderful.

"So there's no single right age," she said slowly, testing the idea like a loose tooth. "There's just a middle and a spread."

"Exactly," Priya said. "Nina worried she was late at eleven. Dia worried she was weird at fourteen. Same family, same parents, totally different."

From downstairs, Dad honked twice. Maya hugged Priya fast, ran to the car, and buckled the rebellious belt without fighting it this time. Leo was still sulking about his game store.

"Hey, Leo," she said. "Want me to argue with the counter guy for you? I'm in the mood to win something."

He sat up straight. "You can try."

Blake sat at the kitchen table with a calculator, two bank statements, and a bag of pretzels he was guarding with his elbow. He had one hundred eighty dollars in his savings account, earned from mowing lawns all summer, and he wanted to know what it would be worth in five years. The bank's letter said his account earned simple interest at six percent, but a flyer tucked inside advertised a new account with compound interest, and it used the word twice without ever saying what it meant.

He worked the simple version first. Six percent of one hundred eighty dollars was ten dollars and eighty cents. Every year, the same ten dollars and eighty cents, like a machine that only knew one trick. Over five years that came to fifty-four dollars, which felt fair but boring. He wrote the total on the back of the flyer: two hundred thirty-four dollars.

The compound account was different, and it took him longer to see why. The first year paid the same ten dollars and eighty cents. But the second year paid interest on one hundred ninety dollars and eighty cents, not on the original amount. He checked it three times, because the extra sixty-five cents looked like a rounding error. By year three the interest payment was bigger than the year before, and by year five his total beat the simple account by almost nine dollars. Nine dollars was two lawn mowings. He sat back and ate a pretzel in a slow, ceremonial way.

"I have to confess something," his sister Priya said from the doorway, sniffing the bag. "I've been eating your pretzels for a week and blaming Dad." Blake had real empathy for Dad, who had apologized twice for something he never did, but he pushed the bag toward her anyway. Peace was worth more than salt.

"Look at this," he said, spinning the flyer toward her. "The compound one grows faster every year because the interest itself earns interest." Then he told her the part that had amazed him most. "The guy at the bank says to divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate to estimate how long money takes to double. Seventy-two divided by six is twelve years. My money doubles in about twelve years."

Priya chewed and did the math on her fingers. "So in twelve years you'll have three hundred sixty dollars, and you'll be twenty-five."

"Rich," Blake said, and then the twist hit him. He frowned at the flyer, turned it over, and read the fine print at the bottom, where the words were too small to be proud of themselves. The compound account's rate was only guaranteed for one year, and after that the bank could change it. The simple account's rate was fixed and written out in explicit terms, no surprises. He tapped the paper twice.

"Maybe boring money is safer money," he said.

Priya stole another pretzel. "Then you'd better hide the bag."

The pickup's air conditioner had given up somewhere outside Tucson, so George kept the window cracked and let the hot wind invade the car, ruffling the rainfall graphs he'd printed for his science project. His dad drove with two fingers on the wheel, and his little sister, Maya, had fallen asleep against a bag of trail mix.

"Ten inches of rain a year," George said to himself, looking at the bar graph for the Sonoran Desert. His pencil hovered over his notes. Back in September he had picked the rainforest for his project because it seemed easy, and he still wondered whether that had been a lazy choice. His teacher had called his last project "influential in all the wrong ways," which George had taken to mean that a poster with a hundred facts was somehow worse than a poster with ten.

He laid the two graphs side by side on his knees. The desert bars were stubby little bricks, barely ten inches stacked up across a whole year. The rainforest bars towered over them, taller than the page almost, month after month. Then he flipped to the third graph, the one that had confused him: a place called Antarctica, all white on the map, snow everywhere, temperatures below freezing half the year. Yet the bars were shorter even than Tucson's.

"There's no way that's a desert," George said out loud. Maya stirred. "It's snowing there right now, probably."

He decided to test it. His rule was simple: he would measure the total rainfall for each place, and if Antarctica came in under ten inches, the graph was calling it a desert whether he liked it or not. He added the bars with his pencil, carrying the ones, checking twice. Tucson: about eleven inches, just over. Antarctica: under ten. Under 250 millimeters, even. He looked at the temperature line and saw it drop below freezing while the rainfall stayed tiny.

"So it counts," he said. "A frozen desert."

Maya woke up long enough to say, "That's not a desert, that's a desert," pointing at the window, where saguaro cactuses stood along the roadside like green posts.

"Both are," George said, and showed her the graph.

They stopped at a pullout above a gray estuary, where the river met the sea and egrets stalked the mud. George got out, paper still in hand, and held both graphs up against the real desert, comparing. A raven landed on a rock nearby and screamed at him.

"Eleven inches," George told it, tapping the Tucson bar. "You're barely making it."

Gabriel had agreed to babysit the Hendersons' eight-month-old, Mia, mostly because the Hendersons' other kid, Ruthie, who was nine, had promised to do all the hard parts. So far the hard parts were real. Mia had dumped a bowl of oatmeal off her high chair tray twice, and now she was refusing the third bowl entirely, pressing her lips shut like a tiny dictator.

"She likes sweet things," Ruthie said, scraping oatmeal off the floor. "Mom puts honey in it sometimes. There's a jar right there."

Gababel reached for the jar on the counter. It was a fat glass bear, and the honey inside moved slow, like it had all day. He was about to twist the lid when Ruthie grabbed a paper off the fridge and held it up so fast it made a snapping sound. The paper said, in Mrs. Henderson's handwriting, NO HONEY FOR MIA. NO HONEY, NO EXCEPTIONS.

"She's nine months old," Ruthie said. "The rule is no honey until after twelve months. Mom says honey can have bacteria spores in it, and they can grow in a baby's gut and make her really sick. It's called infant botulism." She folded her arms, enjoying this. "It's a whole thing."

Gabriel set the bear down. His face went warm, and the embarrassment sat in his stomach like a swallowed rock, because he had almost done it, and because a nine-year-old had caught him. He tried to think of something a babysitter would say. "Good thing I was just, uh, checking the jar for cracks."

"Sure," said Ruthie, who did not believe him at all.

But Mia still wasn't eating, and Gabriel needed her to eat, because Mrs. Henderson came home in an hour and would ask. He looked at the list again. Under the honey warning, in smaller letters, it said Mia likes banana mashed in. So he peeled a banana, mashed it into the oatmeal with a fork, and offered the spoon. Mia considered him with deep suspicion, the way she might consider a large, clumsy stranger who had already dropped her snack twice. Then she inhaled the first bite so fast the spoon came back empty. She kicked both feet and banged the tray for more.

"See," Ruthie said. "Bananas aren't extinct yet."

"That's not what extinct means," Gabriel said.

"I know. I just like the word."

Gabriel fed her the rest of the bowl, one spoonful at a time, while the honey bear sat untouched by the sink, catching the afternoon light like it was proud of itself.

Tyler slid the meatballs across the table to his little cousin Ben before anyone asked, because Ben always wanted what was on the far plate. Their older sister Maren was home from college, and she was watching Ben stack the meatballs into a tower like she was counting them, a slow census of every meatball on the plate.

"Did you take Psych 101 this semester?" Mom asked her.

"Child development, actually," Maren said. "We just covered the Sally-Anne test. It was first used in 1985. Sally puts her marble in a basket and leaves. While she's gone, Anne moves the marble to a box. Then they ask the kid: where will Sally look for her marble?"

"Her basket," Ben said instantly, mouth full.

"Right," Maren said. "Kids from about age four usually say that. She'll look where she left it, not where it was moved while she was away." She grinned. "Ben just passed, sort of."

Tyler put down his fork. Ben was five, so that fit, but something about it bothered him. "Wait. He said basket because he heard the story. That doesn't prove anything."

"Prove what?" Maren said.

"That he understands Sally can believe something false. He might just be tracking where the marble started. That's a different rule."

Dad reached over and refilled Ben's milk without being asked, because Ben was reaching for it with meatball hands. "Sounds like somebody opposes his sister's whole field," he said.

"I'm not opposing it," Tyler said, though he kind of was. "I want to test it. For real."

"Go ahead, genius," Maren said.

Tyler waited until Ben was deep in the meatball tower. He took Ben's favorite green crayon, the one Ben had been drawing with all afternoon, and dropped it into his own cup, the durable blue plastic one that had survived three summers. Then he announced he was getting more bread and walked into the kitchen. Through the doorway he watched Maren quietly slide the crayon into Ben's backpack pocket.

When Tyler came back, he sat down and kept eating. Twenty minutes later, tower demolished, Ben started packing up his drawings. Tyler held his breath.

"Where my green crayon?" Ben scanned the table, then pointed straight at Tyler's blue cup. "Tyler take it."

Tyler's whole idea collapsed right there on the dinner table. He had expected Ben to hunt in the cup, the place the crayon had last been, and had built a little plan around proving Maren's class wrong, or at least proving his own theory right. Instead Ben had read the situation like a detective, tracking not the object but the cousin, and the cousin's history of borrowing things.

"You moved my plan," Tyler told Maren, but he was almost laughing.

"You lost your own test," she said. "Pass the bread."

Ben, meanwhile, had unzipped his backpack to grab his jacket and froze. "Hey. It's in here."

"Want the last meatball?" Tyler asked, sliding it onto Ben's plate. "You earned it, detective."

Jake had one week to learn "Turkey in the Straw" on Grandpa's old fiddle before the family reunion, and so far he could play it exactly as well as he had on Monday, which was badly. He stood in the cluttered back room, rosin dust on his jeans, and played the whole tune through for the ninth time. Nine times, and the same spot still collapsed every single time, right where the notes jumped up quick in the middle of the song.

After dinner he found a worn notebook in the drawer under the sheet music. It had belonged to Grandma, who used to play the same fiddle. Inside, the pages weren't full of whole songs. Instead she had written the same four measures over and over, with little marks and circled notes, and in the margin: "Slow. Again. Slower." Why hadn't she just played her pieces from start to finish? He flipped through page after page and found the same strange pattern everywhere, small chunks with careful notes, almost nothing played all the way through.

He decided to test it. The next morning he ignored the beginning, which he could already play in his sleep, and played only the troublesome jumping section. He played it slowly, then a little faster, then slowly again whenever his fingers tangled. It felt odd, like rehearsing only one line of a joke. But by noon his left hand found the jumps without his eyes, and by evening the whole tune snapped together so smoothly that he played it twice just to hear it happen.

"Do you know what Grandma figured out?" he asked Grandpa at supper. "How you practice, working on your specific weak spots, matters more than just playing the whole piece a bunch of times. That's why she never wrote out full songs."

Grandpa chuckled into his potatoes. "Fifty years of playing and she was the most frugal woman I ever knew, too. Never wasted a single note, on the fiddle or anywhere else."

At the reunion, Jake stood on the porch steps and played the tune all the way through, and the jumping part in the middle, the old troublemaker, sailed by like it had never been hard at all. When he finished, his little cousin tugged his sleeve.

"That was good," she said, "but the best part was the fast part in the middle."

Jake grinned and leaned down to confide the secret. "That part? I played that one more than the rest of the song combined."

The drive to the airport had been awful. Dad took the winding road along the ridge because it was faster, and Norah had spent the whole ride with her novel six inches from her face, which was why, by the time they reached the parking garage, she was green and sweaty and gripping the door handle. Her little brother Theo, who had stared out the window the entire way, bounced out of the car like nothing had happened.

"That's not fair," Norah said, leaning against the suitcase. "You ate three granola bars and you're fine."

"Motion sickness doesn't care about granola bars," Mom said, handing her a water bottle.

At the gate, while Theo played on the carpet with a toy plane, Norah sat very still and thought. She had been reading. Her eyes had been staring at a page, a page that never moves, so her eyes were telling her brain one thing. But the car had been curving and swaying up that road, and something in her inner ear, some balance thing, had been telling her brain the opposite. Her brain had gotten two conflicting stories about whether her body was moving, and she had felt sick. Theo had watched the trees and the guardrail whizzing past, so his eyes and his inner ear were saying the same thing. That had to be it. The idea was vague at first, like a word on the tip of her tongue, but the more she turned it over, the clearer it got.

"Okay," she said out loud. "Test one. On the plane, I read for ten minutes. Then I look out the window for ten minutes. Then I compare."

"Compare what?" Theo asked.

"Whether I feel like throwing up." Theo made a face and went back to his toy plane.

Boarding was the best part so far, the jet bridge humming, the flight attendant saying welcome aboard like she meant it. Norah claimed the window seat and pulled out her book before the plane even pushed back. Her plan to read might hinder her experiment a little, since the plane hadn't started moving yet, but she figured taxiing and takeoff counted.

Ten minutes after they leveled off, her stomach had that familiar wobbly feeling. She marked her page and pressed her forehead to the window. Clouds, a silver river, tiny squares of farmland scrolling past. Her stomach settled, slowly, like water going still.

She spun to Theo. "It works. When your eyes see the movement too, everything agrees, and you feel fine."

Theo held up his toy plane, flying it past her face. "Window seat next time," he said.

Hannah crouched beside trail marker number four with her notebook, two pairs of tweezers, a set of chopsticks, and a paper cup full of seeds she had sorted by size on her bedroom floor. Her project was due Friday: she had to explain how beak shapes on the Galápagos finches had been shaped by natural selection, and she wanted to test it herself instead of just copying facts. Her plan was simple. The big tweezers were the big, crushing beaks. The skinny tweezers were the thin, probing beaks. The chopsticks were, in her opinion, just chopsticks, but she had run out of beak models.

"Are you eating bird food again?" her brother Marcus asked, hiking up behind her with a granola bar. Marcus wanted one thing on these walks, which was to spot a bird before Hannah did, because last month she had beaten him eleven to three and he had not recovered. "Because that's weird even for you."

"It's science." She dumped the large, hard seeds onto the flat rock beside the trail. "Big beaks first." She pinched the big tweezers, picked up a seed, and dropped it into the cup in four seconds. Then she tried the skinny tweezers on the same seeds, and the seed shot off the rock, rolled down the slope, and vanished into a patch of ferns. She recorded both times. When she switched to the tiny soft seeds in the crevice of the rock, the skinny tweezers were quick and nimble while the big ones fumbled like a civilian trying to do surgery with garden shears. The pattern was so clean it almost scared her. Where a food source was restricted to one kind of seed, one beak shape won, every time.

Then a small dark bird landed three feet away and started poking at the fallen seeds. "Blackbird," Marcus said instantly. "I win, that's my bird, point for me."

Hannah looked at it. Curved beak, striped chest, and now that she stared, not really blackbird-shaped at all. "I think it's a finch," she said slowly, and then felt her whole project tip sideways in her head. She had read a paragraph about Darwin and had skipped past a detail that suddenly seemed like the most important thing on the trail. She dug out her book and found the page. In 1837, an ornithologist named John Gould told Darwin that his Galápagos birds, which Darwin had taken for wrens or blackbirds, were actually a new group of closely related finches. Darwin hadn't recognized them either. The whole idea of beaks changing on different islands had come from a correction after the trip, from a scientist back in England who looked closer.

"Wait." Marcus leaned over her shoulder, chewing. "Darwin called them wrens? The evolution guy?" He started laughing so hard he had to sit on the rock. "Okay, fine, I change my vote, it's a finch. But I'm still claiming the point, because I saw it first."

"It's not a contest," Hannah said, already writing. The bird hopped closer, cracked a big seed with a quick sideways motion of its beak, and flew off into the sun.

Zoey kept getting stomachaches before math tests, and today's was the worst yet. Her teacher, Ms. Alvarez, had announced a quiz on the estuary ecosystem, and Zoey's stomach had twisted the moment the words left her mouth.

At lunch, her friend Marcus slid a folded note across the table. "My grandma taught me this," he said. "I couldn't sleep at her house before the science fair, and she got this trick out of a book by a doctor named Andrew Weil."

Zoey unfolded the paper. In Marcus's messy handwriting it read: "It's called 4-7-8 breathing. Breathe in for four counts, hold for seven, breathe out slow for eight. The long breath out is the part that matters. Works best if you practice it at night too, so your body knows the routine. My grandma swears by it. Try it and tell me."

"Four, seven, eight?" Zoey said. "That's weirdly specific."

"So is your face turning green before every quiz," Marcus said, and stole one of her fries.

Zoey decided to test it like an experiment, the way they did in science class. That night she lay in bed and counted silently: in, two, three, four. Hold, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Out, slow, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight. The first few rounds felt silly, like she was blowing up an invisible balloon. But somewhere around the fifth repeat, her shoulders dropped away from her ears, and she fell asleep before she could count how many more she'd done.

She practiced every night that week. She noticed a distinct difference on the third morning: she woke up before her alarm instead of dragging herself out of bed. Her mother even commented that Zoey seemed less grumpy at breakfast, which Zoey chose to take as a compliment.

On Friday, Ms. Alvarez passed out the estuary quiz. Zoey felt the familiar twist begin, so she closed her eyes and counted under her breath. In for four. Hold for seven. Out for eight. When she opened her eyes, her hand was steady enough to write.

After class, she found Marcus at his locker. "It worked," she said. "Stomach didn't stage a rebellion."

"Told you," he said. "Grandma is never wrong. Well, almost never. Don't ask about her gambling on bingo night."

Zoey laughed and wrote a quick reply to his note on the back of her quiz scratch paper: "Four, seven, eight. Officially a believer." She folded it and slid it through the vents of his locker before he could see her grin.

The letter arrived folded inside a seed packet, which was typical of Aunt Rosa. Dear Layla, it read. Congratulations on winning the community garden plot. My gift: corn, beans, and squash seeds, all mixed together on purpose. Plant them the way the old diagram in this envelope shows, and do not argue with me. Love, your aunt, who knows things. Layla held up the diagram. Three circles of dots, a mound in the middle, squash drawn all around like a green puddle. "Who plants three things in one hole?" she asked her friend Marcus, who was leaning on the fence eating a plum.

"That's not a hole, that's a traffic jam," Marcus said. Layla studied the diagram anyway, because her aunt's plans always had a secret inside them. She planted the corn kernels in a cluster at the center of each mound, exactly as the circles showed, and she saved the beans for later, which was the part that made no sense to her at first. Beans climbed things. Corn was a thing. Maybe that was the whole trick, and the squash puddle around the outside was doing something too, though she couldn't see what.

Two weeks later she had her first small fracture in the plan: a rabbit, or possibly Marcus's little brother, had flattened one mound entirely. Layla rebuilt it and wrapped the base of that mound with string, humming as she worked. "You're protecting it," Marcus said. "Trying to preserve the evidence," she said. "When it happens again, I want to know which criminal I'm dealing with." The string stayed untouched for three nights. The rabbit had simply lost interest, which Layla found slightly insulting.

When the corn stood knee-high, she pushed the bean seeds into the soil at its base, and only then did the pattern click. The beans sent out curling tendrils within days and grabbed the corn stalks like tiny green hands looking for a ladder. "They're using the corn as a trellis," Layla said, kneeling in the dirt. Marcus peered down at them. "The corn doesn't mind?" "Aunt Rosa calls it the Three Sisters method," Layla said. "The corn supports the climbing beans, and the squash leaves shade the soil. My aunt says people have planted it this way for centuries."

The part about the squash proved itself without any help from Layla. Her neighbor Mr. Okoye spent every Saturday hacking at weeds with a hoe, his plot bare between rows, while under Layla's sprawling squash leaves the ground stayed dark and nearly empty. She checked by lifting a leaf like a trapdoor, and there was nothing under it but shade. The beans grew so vigorous and heavy that by August the mounds looked like green tents, and the corn leaned together at the top as if huddling over a secret.

In September Aunt Rosa appeared at the garden gate, sunglasses pushed up in her hair. "Well?" she said. Layla handed her a basket: fat beans, golden corn, one squat squash with a dirty smiley face drawn on its skin. "The Three Sisters send their regards," Layla said. Aunt Rosa picked up the squash and studied the face. "Which sister is this one?" "The loud one," said Marcus, from the fence, still eating a plum.

The list went up on the gym door at lunch, and Penelope was tenth in line to see it. The basketball coach had posted the rankings for Player of the Season, one number next to each name, and everyone crowded in to find out where they stood. Dexter, her best friend, pushed forward beside her, chewing the strap of his backpack the way he did when he was nervous. He wanted that award more than he wanted lunch, more than he wanted a snow day, and when he finally spotted his name, his shoulders dropped. He was fourteenth. Fourteenth out of fifteen, because the list counted only one thing, points scored, and Dexter hardly ever shot.

That night Penelope found a letter waiting on her desk, actual paper, folded in thirds. Her uncle had written it after their family dinner at the sports bar on Saturday, when she'd complained that the whole season had been squeezed onto one skinny list of numbers. Dear Penelope, it began. You asked a good question. Here's the story I promised. In 2003 a book came out, "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis. It described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players. A low-budget team, competing against rich teams, because they found players everybody else ignored. He'd signed it with a doodle of a baseball. Penelope read it three times.

At school the next morning she sat in the cafeteria with her notebook and started writing. She had been at every game anyway, keeping score because Coach Ruiz made anyone on the bench supervise the clock. The tallying was tedious, all those little marks, but she had four games of them in her bag. If the Athletics could find hidden value in one statistic, maybe she could too. The question was what to count. Points were what everyone saw. But watching Dexter play, she'd noticed something nobody wrote down: every time he touched the ball, something good tended to happen for the team, even when he never scored.

So she tested it. For every player, she counted touches, and then the times a touch led to a basket, a foul drawn, or a possession kept alive. She called it "good things per touch." She worked through lunch, her pen moving down the columns while the cafeteria roared around her, Marcus and Priya arguing about whether the cafeteria's mystery meat came from a herbivore or a carnivore, which Priya insisted mattered, which Marcus insisted did not. By the time the bell rang, Penelope had one page of numbers and a hollow feeling in her stomach, because something strange was in them.

She didn't tell Dexter. Not yet. She needed the fifth game, the away game on Thursday, to be sure. She rode the bus with the team, notebook on her knees, and marked every touch while the crowd stomped the bleachers. The score stayed close the whole game, tied twice in the last two minutes, and Penelope barely breathed. Dexter got the ball with forty seconds left, everyone in the gym screaming shoot, and he whipped it sideways to Marcus, who was standing alone under the basket. Swish. Then Dexter stole the inbounds pass and got fouled, and made one of two free throws, and the game was over, won by a single point.

On the bus home, under the flickering dome light, Penelope finished her columns and counted the marks one last time, pressing hard with her pencil. She looked up and walked to the seat where Dexter sat with his headphones on, staring out the dark window.

She tapped his shoulder and held the notebook in front of his face, her finger under the final row.

"You're first," she said. "Nobody knows it yet."

Bentley unfolded the agenda he had written the night before and smoothed it against the cafeteria table where the robotics club always met. At the top, in his careful handwriting, it said "Old business, new ideas, snack cleanup," and below that he had copied a note from his notebook: "Last week was a disaster. Nobody could hear Nadia over Dominik."

The meeting started the way his old meetings always started. Dominik talked about the gripper arm, then Marcus talked over Dominik, then two sixth graders argued about wheel size, and the whole discussion seemed to orbit Dominik like he was the sun and everyone else was just passing planets. Bentley clapped twice, which was supposed to be the quiet signal, and nobody quieted at all. Nadia, who sat at the end with her sketchbook, drew a small robot and said nothing.

He remembered then the meeting back in October, when he had let everyone shout ideas freely because it seemed fair. It had not been fair at all. The same three loud people had filled the whole half hour, and Nadia's one attempt at speaking had vanished under Marcus's joke about the club budget, which was in bad shape since the recession had cut the school's funding for supplies. Bentley had told himself that nobody was silenced on purpose. That was exactly the problem, though. It happened without anyone deciding it.

"Okay, stop," Bentley said, standing up. "New rule for today. We're going around the circle. Each person speaks in turn, one at a time, and we don't skip anybody." Dominik groaned, so Bentley added, "It's called a round-robin. It's not optional."

The circle moved slowly at first. Dominik used his whole turn on the gripper arm. Marcus spent his on wheels. The sixth graders split their turn between them. Then it was Nadia's turn, and the room was quiet in a way it had never been quiet before, because everyone was waiting for her instead of talking over her.

She held up her sketchbook. In it was a drawing of the robot driving with the gripper arm extended backward, towing a small cart for the practice field obstacles. "We waste time driving back to the corner for pieces," she said. "If we tow a bin, we can test the whole course without returning." Dominik stared at the page, then at her, then back at the page.
