"That's the most significant idea anyone's had all season," he said, and he actually meant it.

Bentley wrote the round-robin onto the agenda's blank back side, next to a note to try it again next week, and then a question he didn't have an answer to yet: should each turn have a time limit, or would that scare off the quiet people again? He looked down the table. Nadia was already drawing the cart from three angles.

"Same order next meeting?" she asked.

"Same order," Bentley said, and slid the agenda across so she could add her name at the top of the speaking list.

Adam sat in his dad's car outside the gym, and his stomach did a slow flip, like a fish turning over in a bucket. His heart was hammering too, fast and loud, and he hadn't even opened the door yet. Beside him, his best friend Marcus was bouncing one knee against the glove box, which was his own kind of drumbeat.

"You look like you're going to throw up," Marcus said.

"I'm not. It's just that feeling. My stomach's doing backflips and my heart's racing like there's a generator inside my chest running at full speed." Adam stared through the windshield at the stream of kids heading for the doors, laughing, shoving each other, carrying glow sticks that had already been snapped and shook. "And it's weird, because I'm excited. I've been excited all week."

"Then why does your body act like it's an emergency?"

Adam thought about that. In science they'd done a unit on stress, and something clicked into place. "Okay, listen. When you're nervous, your body releases this stuff called adrenaline. It speeds up your heart, and it pulls blood away from your stomach." He tapped his own stomach. "That's the butterflies. That's all it is. Your stomach's just not getting the blood."

Marcus squinted at him. "You made that up."

"Ask Ms. Rivera Monday. But think about it. I'm nervous about the dance, so adrenaline kicks in, my heart goes fast, and my stomach flips because the blood got pulled somewhere else. Butterflies. It's not me actually being sick. It's a pattern, and once you know the pattern, you can outsmart it."

Marcus's knee was still going. "How do you outsmart butterflies?"

"That's the part I want to test." Adam reached for the door handle. "My theory is that if I just get in there and start moving, the nerves will burn off. Sitting still insulates them. Like keeping them warm and safe. Moving breaks them up."

"You sound like a health video," Marcus said, but he was grinning, and the grin was infectious, spreading to Adam even before they were out of the car. Marcus had his own mission tonight anyway: he'd promised the student council he'd get twenty kids to sign up for the spring talent show, and he'd brought a clipboard and three pens in his jacket pocket. He wanted to be the guy who made it happen.

They crossed the parking lot at almost a jog, weaving between cars still ticking as they cooled. At the doors, the music hit them like a wave, and Adam felt his heart give one more huge thump. He decided to treat it as the starting gun. Inside, under the spinning lights, he grabbed Marcus's sleeve, pulled him straight onto the dance floor, and started the worst, boldest dancing of his entire life. Marcus held up his clipboard and shouted over the music, "First signature goes to you!"

Nicholas sat cross-legged on Dev's bedroom floor with Dev's phone glowing between them, watching the new class group chat scroll like a slot machine. Forty-two people, and Mr. Rivas hadn't said who was in charge of it, so the chat had already produced three memes, one argument about cafeteria pizza, and a photo of someone's hamster wearing a tiny hat. "We should nominate someone to set rules," Dev said, typing nothing because he was too busy laughing at the hamster. Nicholas frowned at the screen. Could a chat even have official manners, the kind somebody actually wrote down, like a handbook?

He borrowed his own phone from his pocket and typed the wondering question straight into the search bar: did anyone ever write official online manners? The first serious result looked strange, like a document from a filing cabinet in a basement. It was published in 1995, which was so long ago that his parents had probably been kids arguing about their own group chats, except there weren't any. "It's called the 'Netiquette Guidelines'," Nicholas read aloud, "and it's a document called RFC 1855." Dev leaned over. "RFC? What does that stand for?" "No idea," Nicholas admitted, which somehow made it more interesting, like a treasure map with the corners torn off.

They scrolled through it together. Some advice sounded ancient, all-caps meant shouting even back then, before anyone Nicholas knew had been born. Some advice sounded like it had been written about their chat that very morning. There was a part about how the same message can land differently depending on where you send it, private to one person versus public to everyone, which gave Nicholas a theory. "I bet that's the pizza fight," he said. "Marco typed a joke, and Priya read it in front of everybody, so it stopped being a joke." It was a hidden cause, invisible, the kind of thing you couldn't see, only test.

Dev's little sister barged in without knocking, which was its own lesson about public and private spaces, and demanded to know why they were reading a rulebook for fun. "It's not a rulebook, it's suspense," Dev told her grandly. "We don't know if it works." Nicholas decided to run the test right there. He sent Marco a private message: hey, was the pizza thing a joke? Then he waited, and waiting for a reply, he decided, was the true spontaneous version of suspense, worse than any movie. The reply buzzed back in eleven seconds: obviously?? I love cafeteria pizza. I would marry cafeteria pizza.

Nicholas pasted that into the main chat, and Marco added a pizza emoji, and Priya replied with a laughing face and the hamster photo again, and the argument dissolved so completely that it was almost suspicious, like it had never really existed. Dev nominated the hamster for chat president, and someone seconded it. Nicholas looked down at the search result still open on his screen, a document older than everyone in the room, quietly fixing things twenty-eight years later. "Okay," he said, holding up the phone so Dev could see it. "But if the hamster wins, we're looking up whether RFC 1855 covers tiny hats."

Isabelle crouched in aisle four of Holloway's Garden Center, holding a carrot seed packet in one hand and a bean packet in the other. The packets felt papery and old, and the air smelled like wet soil and green tomato vines. She had one week before the county's junior grower contest, which required proof that a vegetable had been planted and sprouted by the entry deadline.

"Carrots by Saturday, huh?" said Marcus, balancing a bag of potting mix on his shoulder. "That's fast."

"The contest just needs them planted and sprouted," Isabelle said. "The rules permit sprouted seeds, not full plants. So they only have to poke up out of the dirt." She shook the carrot packet. Inside, the seeds rattled like sand. She tore the corner and shook one into her palm. It was flat and tiny, smaller than a comma in a book. Marcus opened the bean packet and tipped out a seed the size of his thumbnail, wrinkled and brown.

She frowned. Back in the spring she had planted beans in her grandmother's garden, dropping each one into a hole deep enough to bury a marble. The beans had come up in a week, fat and green. But her grandmother had also shown her a trick for carrots, barely scratching the soil surface and dusting the seeds over like pepper. "Carrots get a sprinkle," Gran had said, tapping the packet. "Beans get a real hole." Isabelle turned both seeds over in her palm and squinted at them.

"I think I see it," she said slowly. "A seed goes in about two to three times as deep as it is wide. Look. This bean is this big around." She held up her thumb and finger, spaced apart. "So it goes in about that deep, maybe a little more. And the carrot seed is barely anything, so it goes in barely anything at all. Almost on top." Marcus leaned in and compared the two seeds side by side, then nodded like something had clicked.

They bought both packets with Isabelle's birthday money and raced home before the rain. In the backyard, Marcus dug bean holes with two fingers while Isabelle pressed each bean in about twice its own width and patted the soil firm. For the carrots she scattered the seeds across the bed and sifted a whisper of dirt over them, no thicker than the seeds themselves. They watered gently so the tiny ones wouldn't wash away, and every evening afterward Isabelle patrolled the bed with a flashlight after dark, checking for slugs, which were nocturnal and always left slimy trails on the leaves by morning.

On the sixth day, the rain stopped long enough for sun. Isabelle knelt at the carrot bed and saw them: hundreds of hair-thin green threads, bent like tiny question marks, pushing out of the soil. The beans had already unfurled their first pair of leaves, fat and cheerful. She ran inside, grabbed the contest entry form, and wrote the date at the top. Then she carried her phone out to the garden, knelt down, and took a photo of the sprouts glistening in the morning light. "Look at you," she whispered. "Come on, carrots. Grow."

Lea had spent all Saturday getting the guest bedroom ready, because Grandma Ruth was coming for a whole week. She put fresh sheets on the bed, a stack of mysteries on the dresser, and a lamp angled toward the armchair where Grandma liked to read. At dinner that first night they talked for two hours, about school and about Great-Aunt Fern's terrible casserole, and Grandma caught every word, even when Lea mumbled the punchline of a joke.

On Wednesday they went to meet Lea's mom at the train station, since her train got in at five. The station café was packed, with espresso machines hissing and announcements rolling overhead. Lea told Grandma about the science fair, and Grandma leaned in and said, "The air bear? What bear?" Lea repeated it louder. Grandma laughed, but it was the wrong laugh, the kind that covers a miss. By the time Mom walked up, Grandma had gone quiet and was stirring a coffee she hadn't sipped.

That night Lea sat on the guest bed with her notebook. At home, Grandma heard everything. At the station, she missed almost everything. The difference wasn't Grandma's ears getting worse in one afternoon; it was where they were. Something about the noise itself was swallowing the words. She wrote: maybe Grandma's hearing is like hers, but biased toward trouble in loud places, so what she needs is a fair test. Same Grandma, same sentences, different room. She'd pivot the experiment to the kitchen in the morning, quiet first, then noisy, and see if the pattern held.

At breakfast, in the silent kitchen, Lea said casually, "The science fair is Friday." Grandma said, "You'll do great, sweetheart," and asked what Lea's project was, which meant the words had landed. Then Lea turned on the radio, the blender, and the dishwasher all at once, and asked, "What time does Mom's train leave Saturday?" Grandma squinted and said, "Purple? The purple what?" Lea shut everything off. Same question in the quiet got an instant, correct answer. The rule was plain now: loud rooms erased speech for Grandma even when the words themselves were easy.

Lea left a note on the guest bedroom pillow that evening. "Dear Grandma, I figured out the station. It wasn't you missing things, it was the noise eating the words. From now on we'll talk in the quiet corners, and I'll write the important stuff down. Love, Lea." Under it she listed Saturday's train time in big letters.

The next day they met Mom at the station again. This time Lea steered Grandma past the café to a bench at the far end of the platform, where only trains passed and only sometimes. "Mom's coming on the six o'clock," Lea said. Grandma nodded, relaxed, and asked whether Lea would participate in the talent show this spring, the one she'd barely caught a word about on Wednesday. When the six o'clock slid in, Mom waved from the doors and Grandma waved back, and said, "This spot is better. How did you know?" Lea held up her notebook, open to the page with the radio and the blender scrawled at the top.

Tyler sat on Marcus's bedroom floor with the phone glowing in his hands, scrolling up and down the same conversation for the third time. It was a thread with Jayla, started two days ago, and something about it had gone wrong, though he could not point to where.

"Read this," he said, holding the screen out to Marcus. The last message said Okay. That's fine. See you Monday.

Marcus squinted at it. The translucent curtain shifted in the window breeze, throwing pale light across the screen. "What am I looking at?"

"She's mad at me. I can feel it. But look at the words. They're fine."

"Then she's not mad."

"She didn't answer my last three texts for a whole day, and when she did answer, it had periods in it. Every sentence. Period, period, period." Tyler tapped the screen. "When she's normal, she writes like okay and lol see u. No periods anywhere."

Marcus leaned back against his bed and laughed. "You're mad because of punctuation."

"You don't get it. It's a different tone. It's like she's texting me from inside a glass box." Tyler remembered the fight they'd had last summer, the one he still wasn't sure he should have walked away from, and how she'd ended that argument with a single word and a period too. He had thought about that message more times than he wanted to admit.

Marcus pulled out his own phone and typed for a minute, then turned it around. On the screen was an article about a small 2016 study by researchers at Binghamton University. "It says messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one," Marcus read. "They tested it. People actually judged the periods."

"So I'm not crazy."

"You're not crazy. You're just dramatic." Marcus dropped the phone on the carpet. "So what are you going to do, eliminate the periods and pretend nothing happened?"

Tyler stared at the message thread. His thumb hovered over the keyboard. He could send a joke, or he could send the question he'd been avoiding since June, the one about whether walking away had been the right call. A joke would smooth it over. A question might start something he couldn't stop, like an infection that spreads through a whole friendship before you notice the first symptom.

He typed: You sounded mad in that last text. Are we okay?

He read it twice, deleted the period at the end, and sent it before he could change his mind. The typing bubble appeared almost instantly.

Antoine sat at the kitchen computer with the town's website open and his grandma's pill bottle next to the mouse. She had just taken her prescription and gone to the porch, which meant he had the whole afternoon to settle the argument. Yesterday Marcus had said, in front of everyone, that Ridgeway was founded in 1848 by a man named Silas Crane, and he'd pointed at the town website as proof. Antoine wanted to knock that down, because the big sign at the library said 1851.

He clicked through the site again. Founded 1848, it said, right there under "Our Proud History." Antoine groaned. Maybe Marcus was right after all. But something bothered him. The site also said the first school was built of brick, and Antoine had seen a photograph in the library of a wooden school. If the site could be wrong once, it could be wrong twice.

Grandma had shown him the county archive last month, a website full of scanned old newspapers. He typed in the address and started digging. He decided to exclude anything written after 1900, because a paper from 1960 telling the story was just repeating what somebody else had said. He wanted stuff from the actual time. He found a clipping from 1852 reporting the town's founding day celebration, "our first anniversary," and an official county record listing the plat of Ridgeway filed in 1851 by Silas Crane. There it was, in the town's own paper, written when the town was young enough to remember.

Marcus came over at four o'clock, still grinning. "You find anything, or did you just look at the website again?"

"The website's wrong," Antoine said. He turned the screen so Marcus could see the 1852 clipping. "This is a primary source. It's a firsthand record from the time, like a letter, a photograph, or official data. It's the best place to check a claim."

Marcus leaned in and read the yellowed column twice. His grin faded, then came back, but different now. "Huh. So Crane did found it, just three years later than everybody says."

"Maybe the website writer got it from a book that got it wrong," Antoine said. "My grandpa's old boxes of clippings are in the basement, and Dad keeps them away from the flammable furnace, so they're all still readable. We could look through those too."

Marcus pulled a chair up next to him. "First we email the town office."

Antoine opened his inbox and started typing. He attached the clipping, and his finger hovered over the send button. Then he clicked it, and the little confirmation chime rang out across the kitchen.

Cameron had planned to spend the whole week building a fort in the backyard, but on Saturday his grandpa arrived with two suitcases and a folding cot, and the fort plans got stacked in the garage next to the tent poles. Grandpa was sleeping in the den, and the den was where Cameron kept his good hammer. He felt a small, hot knot of resentment about it, which he did not mention, because Grandpa had brought a bag of licorice and was already telling a story about a horse that got into a church.

On Monday morning they were outside early, because Grandpa liked to sit in the lawn chair before the sun could radiate any real heat off the fence. The backyard flowerbed was bone dry and arid after weeks without rain, and Grandpa tapped the cracked dirt with his shoe and said the marigolds were on their own. Then he frowned. "Did I take my morning pills or didn't I? I've asked myself that three times now, and I don't trust the answer."

Cameron went inside to look. On the kitchen counter sat a plastic box with seven little lids in a row, labeled S, M, T, W, T, F, S. Each compartment held a small pile of pills. The Monday lid was open and the Monday compartment was empty. Cameron carried the box outside and held it up. "The box has one compartment for each day of the week," he said. "Monday's empty, so you already took Monday's pills." Grandpa peered at it, then laughed. "A pill box with a memory in it. Better than me." He did not take any more pills.

By Tuesday, Grandpa was checking with Cameron every morning, and by Wednesday it had become a routine, like feeding the dog. Cameron started filling the box himself on Sunday nights, counting out the pills from the bottles, snapping each little lid shut. Grandpa called him "the pharmacist" and paid him one jellybean per day, which Cameron considered a bad rate but accepted.

Thursday morning, though, the Thursday compartment was already empty at seven a.m., before Grandpa had eaten anything. Cameron stood at the counter and thought. Then he went outside and found Grandpa's coffee cup on the fence post, and next to it, on the ground, four small white pills sitting in the dust. The dog, Biscuit, was licking her lips nearby. "Grandpa," Cameron called, "did you drop your pills anywhere?" Grandpa patted his shirt pocket, his pants pocket, and finally pointed at the fence post. Cameron held up the four pills he had picked out of the dirt. "You took them out and set them down, and I think Biscuit was faster than you."

Grandpa put his hand over his heart like a man receiving terrible news. "That dog," he said, "is stealing my medicine and my reputation." He swallowed the pills with a drink from the garden hose, and Cameron went back inside to write DOG on a piece of tape and stick it on the fence post, right where the Thursday pills had sat.

The vase had been on the windowsill since September, blue with a chipped rim, and on Monday morning it lay in pieces on the floor. Mrs. Alvarez stood over the shards with her coffee mug in one hand and said, "Nobody's in trouble. I just want to know what happened."

Abigail's mind was already running through the possibilities. Dylan said he'd seen Marcus back there before first bell, reaching toward the window. Marcus insisted he'd only been closing the blinds because the sun was in his eyes. Priya claimed she heard a thump while she was at her locker, which meant the vase fell before Dylan even walked in. And Rosa said flatly that the window had been open and the wind must have knocked it off, though the night before had been dead calm.

"I don't get it," Abigail whispered to Priya. "They can't all be true, but they all sound so sure."

That certainty bothered her the most. Last winter, when she had the flu, her father had put on an old movie to keep her company on the couch, Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon. Four witnesses described one crime, a samurai's death, and every single account contradicted the others. Her father had let her watch the whole thing without saying a word, and when it ended she'd asked, "So which one lied?" He'd only shrugged. She'd spent three days thinking about it before she understood that the real answer might be that none of them were exactly lying, and none were exactly right.

She raised her hand. "Quick question for everyone who was in the room. What color was the vase?"

"Blue," said Rosa and Priya together.

"Green," said Dylan.

Marcus said, "White, I think. Sort of whitish."

Mrs. Alvarez emphasized each word as she repeated it. "The vase was blue." She set down her mug and pulled up the attendance screen. "Marcus, Dylan, you were both in the hallway by the water fountain. Priya, you were at your locker down the hall. Rosa, you came in first." She paused. "Rosa, did you touch the shelf?"

Rosa's chin came up. "I moved it two inches. The sun was going to crack it someday anyway. I didn't think it would just fall."

"Two inches toward the edge," Mrs. Alvarez said quietly.

Rosa stared at the shards, and Abigail realized something else, too: Rosa had opened the window to air out the room, then forgotten, and the wind she denied had come later, after the vase was already teetering. Two half-true stories stacked on top of each other, like the ones in her father's movie.

"You're not in trouble," Mrs. Alvarez said again, softer this time. "But next time, just tell me the whole thing."

Rosa knelt and began picking up the blue pieces one by one.

On Saturday morning, Charlotte slid into her chair at the kitchen table and stared at the small white box beside her cereal. Her mother had left it there with a sticky note that read "After breakfast," which was the crueldest thing anyone had ever written, because how was a person supposed to eat with a phone box sitting eight inches from her elbow?

At the phone store, a kid named Theo was waiting too, dragging his dad toward the display cases. "I wonder how long people have even had phones in their pockets," Theo said, poking a demo model. "Like, did cave people text?" His dad sighed in a way that suggested this was not the first question of the day.

The saleswoman grinned. "The first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by Motorola engineer Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973," she said, tapping the counter like she was announcing a sports score. Theo's jaw dropped. Charlotte filed that away, because it felt like the kind of fact that could win an argument someday, possibly against her little brother.

Back at the kitchen table, Charlotte set up the phone with the concentration of a scientist handling dangerous plumbing. One wrong move and something might leak, except instead of water it would be her entire screen time. Her mother watched over her shoulder. "Sixty minutes on school nights," she said. "I need you to reassure me that you can live with that."

"Mom," Charlotte said, holding the phone like a rare artifact, "in 1973, Martin Cooper made a phone call on a street in New York. One call. He was a Motorola engineer, and it was April third, and it was the first call ever from a handheld cellular phone. People back then survived with one call. I can survive sixty minutes." Her mother laughed so hard she had to sit down, which Charlotte took as a good sign.

But then came the test. Charlotte had an idea. If the phone was really hers to manage, she could prove it, so she set a timer, put the phone face down at the edge of the table, and read an entire chapter of her book while the clock ran out. When the timer buzzed, she switched the phone off herself, without being asked, and slid it into the drawer with the measuring cups. The kitchen went strangely tranquil, just the hum of the refrigerator and the last page turning.

Her mother peeked around the doorframe. "You turned it off. Voluntarily." Charlotte held up her book. "Tomorrow I'm going to call Theo and tell him the Cooper fact again, and also that I finished a whole chapter. He's going to be so jealous."

Chase sat at the long table in his uncle's study, where the afternoon light fell across a book propped on a wooden stand. In three weeks he would read from the Torah for his bar mitzvah, and every word had to come from memory, because the scroll itself had no vowels, no punctuation, nothing but letters. He had practiced the passage forty times at home, but here, in front of the real parchment, the words kept sliding out of his head like water off a roof.

"Again," said Uncle Ezra, who was not really his teacher, just the relative who happened to know the cantillation marks better than anyone else in the family. "From the second verse."

Chase began, and this time the melody came, the little rises and drops he had drilled until they felt automatic. His uncle had told him that repetition builds the reading into your memory the way a path wears into grass, gradual and invisible until one day it is simply there. Chase had learned in science class that practice strengthens connections between one neuron and the next, and he liked imagining the path forming inside him, even though he could never actually watch it happening.

Then his finger, moving on its own, drifted toward the scroll. He wanted to point at the exact spot where he kept tripping over a word, to pin it down like a bug in a jar. Uncle Ezra reached over without a word and set something in his palm: a slim silver rod with a tiny hand at the end, fingers curled, one extended.

"Use the yad," his uncle said. "Yad means hand."

Chase turned it over, wondering why the pointer was shaped like the very thing it replaced. He touched the parchment with one fingertip, just to understand, and felt how thin it was, soft and alive somehow, nothing like paper. His uncle's face didn't change, but Chase noticed how carefully the scroll had been dressed, wrapped in velvet, belted, shielded, as if it were something that could be hurt. Was that the reason? He didn't ask. He laid the yad's little finger against the line instead and read the verse straight through, no stumble, and the problem word sat quietly under the silver hand like it had been waiting to behave.

They read the whole passage twice more, and the second time Chase closed his eyes for a full line and the words were still there, worn into him like the path in the grass. When he opened them, his uncle was smiling.

"Three weeks," Uncle Ezra said, "and you're already pointing like a professional."

Kaitlyn sat on the low wall by the swings with her right arm propped on her knee, the cast gone gray at the edges from two weeks of playground dust. Across the blacktop, the eighth graders were choosing teams for four square, and Marcus had already called her spot. She wanted that spot back. The trouble was that her arm was sealed away, and she could not see a single thing that was happening inside it.

She tried an experiment anyway. She pressed two fingers of her left hand along the cast, right where Dr. Okafor had drawn a small arrow on the fiberglass, marking the place the bone had snapped. Then she wiggled the fingers of her casted hand, slow, then fast, then slow again. They cooperated perfectly. She flexed her wrist as far as the stiff shell allowed. Not perfect, but close. That meant the tendons were fine, she reasoned, but it told her nothing about the bone itself, which was the part that actually had to heal. Something could be mending under there, or not, and no amount of wiggling would show it. She needed the follow-up appointment, and that was still three days away.

The appointment came on Thursday. In the exam room, the X-ray machine hummed, and then a new picture of her arm glowed on the light box beside the old one. Kaitlyn leaned in. On the first film, the bone ended in a clean, dark break, like a snapped pencil. On the new one, there was a fuzzy lump sitting right across the gap, a soft gray cloud where the sharp line used to be.

"See that?" Dr. Okafor said, tapping the lump with the end of a pen. "That's your callus."

"What's it made of?" Kaitlyn asked.

The doctor turned to her chart. "Cartilage and new bone," she said, writing something down. "It bridges the gap between the broken ends." Then she was out the door to the next patient, and Kaitlyn was left staring at the cloud. She had assumed healing would look like the bone knitting itself edge to edge, neat and invisible. Instead her body had built a lump first, a scaffold she could never have felt or seen from the outside. That was why her probing fingers had found nothing. The repair was happening in there anyway, steadily, whether she checked on it or not.

She thought about this on the walk to school the next morning. She had been treating healing like a negotiation, as if enough motivation and daily wiggling could speed it up. It was more like the four square rule nobody questioned: the ball must bounce once before you hit it. You could argue all you wanted, but the rule kept working the same way with or without you. Her arm, she decided, was probable to be ready by the tournament in two weeks, not because she wanted it, but because the callus said so.

At lunch, Marcus waved her over to the blacktop. "You're back! Want your corner?"

Kaitlyn bounced the ball once, then twice, testing her grip. "Actually," she said, "I reffed four square for two weeks with this arm. I know every dirty move you people make."

Marcus groaned. "That's exactly why we didn't want you reffing."

"Too late," Kaitlyn said, and planted herself at the center square with the ball under her good arm. "First serve. No doubles, no arguing, and Marcus, I saw that spin last Tuesday."

"The ref has a cast on," Marcus told the fourth square, "and she's still beating us."

"Whistle hand works fine," said Kaitlyn, and bounced the ball into his square so hard it spun twice before he touched it.

"Out!" she called, before it even landed.

The quiz cards were taped beside the tanks, and whoever answered the most correctly by lunch would win a spot on the behind-the-scenes tour. Jack had his heart set on that tour, because the aquarium's newest harbor seal pup was being raised off display and only the tour group would get to see her. He was three for three until he reached the last card, near the jellyfish tank, where the question read: "True or false: every cow in a dairy barn has had a calf."

"False," Jack said immediately, and reached for the pencil.

"Wait," said Priya, who had been trailing him from tank to tank all morning. "Don't just pick something random. Think about it." She nodded toward the harbor seal pool, where a mother seal was nursing her pup. "See how she's making milk for the baby? My family used to board our horse next to a dairy farm, and I never once saw a cow being milked that didn't have a calf somewhere."

Jack frowned. He had been picturing the stereotypical dairy barn from television, rows of calm black-and-white cows giving milk all day, every day, forever. But if milk existed to feed a baby, then a cow would only have it after a calf was born. He tried to find a hole in the idea and couldn't. "So the answer is true," he said slowly. "Every single one of them." He erased his answer, changed it, and handed the card to the volunteer at the desk.

"Correct," the volunteer said, sorting the cards. "That's the one most people miss." Jack had been ready to resign himself to losing the tour, and now he was jumping like the sea otter two tanks over. Priya laughed and punched his shoulder, and the two of them followed the guide through a plain gray door marked Staff Only.

The guide led them down a corridor that smelled of fish and bleach, past freezers and hoses, and stopped at a low pool. The seal pup lay on the wet concrete beside her mother, blinking at them with round dark eyes. "She's growing fast," the guide said, "because her mom's making plenty of milk for her. Same as out at your farms, right?" Jack looked at Priya, and they both grinned. "Told you," she whispered. "Nobody makes milk without a baby." Jack leaned closer as the pup flopped toward the water, and the mother nudged her in with her nose.

Cole's grandmother had left the bottle of mystery liquid on the counter with a sticky note that read, "Science experiment? Don't drink it." She had also left a box of small paper strips that turned colors, which she called litmus paper, and a chart with numbers from zero to fourteen. Cole wanted to impress her by figuring out what the liquid was before she came home from the garden club. If the strip turned red, it was an acid. If it turned blue, it was a base. Somewhere in the middle, around seven, it was neutral, like water.

He arranged everything on the kitchen table like a lab bench. He had a cup of water, a splash of lemon juice his mom kept in the fridge, and a bit of baking soda dissolved in another glass, so he could practice on things he already knew. "Test the known stuff first," he said to himself, because that was what scientists on TV always did. He dipped a strip into the lemon juice. It turned pink, fast, like the paper was blushing. The chart said lemon juice sat low on the scale, around two.

He tried the baking soda water. The strip went blue, and the chart put it above seven, closer to nine. So far the paper had never lied to him. He felt ready, almost too ready, and in a vain attempt to look like a professional, he put on his dad's safety goggles even though the mystery liquid was probably just soap. When he finally dipped a fresh strip into the unlabeled bottle, he held his breath.

The strip did not turn all red or all blue. It turned purple, then shifted toward blue at the tip and pink in the middle, as if it could not make up its mind. Cole leaned closer. The chart only made sense if the whole strip matched, and this one looked like two answers fighting. He remembered the note on the box, small print he had skipped: "Vinegar and drain cleaner spilled near the sink." Maybe the bottle had gotten contaminated. He decided to run a test, because guessing was useless. He dipped a clean strip into plain water, then touched one end of it to the mystery liquid and watched the color crawl.

The blue crept up the wet strip like a slow laser beam filling a dark room, one millimeter at a time. Where it stopped, the purple held its line. The liquid was a base, but a weak one, and the water had diluted it, which explained the mixed colors. His test had worked. Then he heard the back door, and his grandmother came in with dirt on her hands.

"That mystery liquid was just my homemade window cleaner," she said, laughing. "The real question is whether you learned anything."

"Did you know litmus paper comes from lichens?" Cole asked. "Those are the crusty growths you find on rocks and tree bark. I read the box. There's a whole patch of that stuff on your garden wall."

His grandmother looked out the window at the gray crust on the stones. "So the wall has been making science supplies this whole time," she said, and set the bottle of window cleaner down next to the purple strip.

The computer lab smelled like warm plastic, and Madison had exactly one problem: her best friend Priya had gone silent for three days, and the only clue was a photo Priya had posted of herself on a porch, grinning, with the caption "guess where." Everyone in the comments was guessing. Nobody had guessed right.

Madison opened the photo and dragged it to fill the screen. Priya stood on wooden steps, holding a mug. Behind her was a railing, a bush, and the edge of a door. The caption said nothing about place. But in the corner of the shot, half cut off, stood a green sign with white letters. Madison zoomed in until the pixels blurred, then sharpened the image with the lab's editing software. Elm Street. On the door behind Priya, a brass number was just readable: 47.

She sat back. She had never thought about how a photo could tell a stranger where it was taken, but now it seemed obvious. A street sign, a house number, even a school logo on a hoodie in the background could let someone work out the exact spot. Anyone scrolling could do what she had just done. She thought of the mechanism of it, how the camera caught everything, not just the smile but the whole background, and how a post could be shared onward to people neither of them knew, and stored even after it was deleted.

Priya walked into the lab ten minutes later, dumped her bag, and slid into the seat beside her. "You solved it yet?"

"Elm Street, house forty-seven," Madison said. "Your aunt's porch."

Priya's mouth opened. "How did you do that?"

"Your sign. And the number on the door. You have to crop that stuff out before you post, or anyone can find where you live."

Priya leaned over and looked at the zoomed photo for a long moment. "I'm taking it down. And I'm going through everything I've ever posted." She pulled out her phone and started deleting, her thumb working fast, as if the old photos were something corrosive eating at the screen.

The lab door opened and their teacher came in carrying a stack of permission forms. She held one up. "Priya, your aunt called. She says thanks for the lovely photo of her house, but next time maybe don't post the address, because three of her old students showed up on the porch yesterday."

"Three?" said Priya.

"Former students," the teacher said. "She taught at Elm Elementary for twenty years. The sign behind you is on the school's website."

Madison looked at the green sign in the photo and laughed. "I thought I discovered something. Turns out the whole internet already knew where you were."

"Delete," said Priya, and pressed the button.

Victoria had measured her bean plants every morning for two weeks, and the numbers had gone flat. The plants sat on the sill above the kitchen sink, and every one of them had stopped at eleven centimeters. She wrote "plateau" in her notebook and underlined it twice, because it looked official.

Her brother Dev leaned over her shoulder. "Dad says science is when you get proved right."

"I don't think that's it," Victoria said. She had a science fair in nine days and a table full of stalled beans, and she needed a better answer than that.

The problem was the water. She couldn't see what was in it, either way, but the plants in her bedroom, the ones her friend Amara had watered with bottled water during a visit, had kept growing. So Victoria made a guess and wrote it at the top of a fresh page: the tap water is what stopped the beans. She split the sink plants into two groups, A and B, and gave group A bottled water only.

"Even if they grow, how do you know it was the water?" Dev asked. "Maybe they were just going to start again anyway."

That was the question that ruined her afternoon. She stared at the notebook while the washing machine thumped in the hallway and the beans sat there being stalled and useless. Her idea was a guess, but it needed to be a guess that could lose.

In the study she found their dad's old college paperback, The Logic of Scientific Discovery, spine cracked, margins full of his handwriting. She flipped it open and read a page, then read it again. A philosopher named Karl Popper had argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea was scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong. She copied the sentence onto an index card, including the date, because the judge at last year's fair was the kind of person who asked for dates.

At dinner she tested it on Dev. "If my beans were going to start growing again no matter what, my water idea is wrong. That's the point. There has to be something that could prove it wrong, or it's not really science." She speared a piece of broccoli. "Popper said that. Nineteen thirty-four."

"Sounds easy to humiliate your idea, then," Dev said.

"That's what makes it good," Victoria said.

For six days she watered group A with bottled water and group B from the tap, same amount, same time of day, ruler every morning. On day four, group A had gained a centimeter and a half. Group B sat at eleven. By day six, group A had small curling tendrils reaching for the window, and when she pulled one sick plant from group B to check the roots, she found them brown and stubby, nothing like group A's intricate white threads.

At the fair, the judge stopped at her poster and read the whole thing, top to bottom, with her arms crossed. "Nice growth data," she said. "So tell me. What result would have shown your idea was false?"

"If both groups had stayed stalled," Victoria said. "Or if both had grown. Either one would have proved the water didn't matter."

The judge wrote something on her clipboard, then pointed at the index card taped beside the graph. "Where'd you find Popper?"

"My dad's shelf," Victoria said, and squared the poster against the table edge.

Tyler had agreed to the neighborhood cleanup mostly because his friend Marcus promised there would be donuts, but when he signed in at the community center, the volunteer coordinator steered him toward the food bank tables instead of the park with the trash grabbers. "We're short-handed on sorting today," she said, handing him a pair of gloves. The room smelled of cardboard and canned peaches.

His job was simple. Check each donated item, wipe it down, and put it on the right shelf: canned goods here, pasta there, cereal on the tall rack by the window. He liked the rhythm of it, and he started noticing patterns. Tuna cans lasted for years, judging by the dates. Pasta lasted a long time too. But cereal boxes had dates that were much closer, and half of them were already past.

Across the table, a woman named Rosa picked up a box of oat cereal, frowned, and dropped it into the discard bin. Tyler watched her do the same thing to the next box. Something about it bothered him. The boxes were sealed, undented, not even stale-smelling through the plastic inner bag. Why would perfectly good cereal get thrown away when the banged-up cans stayed?

"Those are only one day past the date," he said, fishing a box out of the bin. Rosa glanced at the printed date and shrugged. "Past is past," she said. "You don't want to give people expired food." Tyler turned the box over in his hands. The date didn't say "expired," though. It said "best if used by." He asked Rosa what she thought that meant. She hesitated. "That it goes bad after?"

That didn't sit right with him. Tyler went to the break room, borrowed the old laptop, and searched the phrase. The USDA's own words came up on the screen: a "best if used by" date shows when a food will be at its best quality; it is not a food-safety date. He read it twice, then carried the laptop back and set it in front of Rosa. She leaned in, squinting, then straightened up slowly. "Huh," she said. "So it's about taste, not about making anyone sick." "That's what it says," Tyler said. "So that cereal isn't dangerous. It's just maybe not at its peak anymore." He wondered out loud how many boxes had been tossed over the years for that exact reason, some hidden rule nobody had ever checked.

They tested the idea together, opening one dated box from the discard bin. The cereal snapped when Tyler bit a piece, crisp and plain, maybe a little less exciting than fresh. They sorted the rest back onto the shelf, and by noon the rack by the window was full again. The coordinator walked past and stopped, staring at the pile of reclaimed boxes. "Where did all this come from?" she asked. Tyler held up the oat cereal, one day past its date, and grinned. "Breakfast," he said.

The gym smelled like floor wax and sweat, and Grayson's legs were already shaking before the second drill even started. Coach Reyes had posted the tryout list on the door: twenty-two boys, twelve spots. Grayson caught the ball at the three-point line, squared up, and bricked it off the back rim. His fatigue was getting in the way, and he knew it, but knowing didn't make his arms any lighter. On the sideline, leaning against the bleachers, sat his neighbor Dana in her swim parka, towel around her neck. Her swim tryout was in the school pool at four o'clock, the exact same time as his, so she had chosen to come watch his first hour and miss the warm-up lap times.

"Nice brick," she called, and he jogged past her on the way to the water station.

"You're one to talk," he said. "You're going to walk into your tryout cold." He didn't add what he was really thinking, which was that last spring he had skipped her district meet to go shoot hoops at the park, and she had found out, and neither of them had ever said anything about it. Some things felt almost permanent even when nobody mentioned them.

Between drills, while the other boys ran lines, Dana showed him her phone. "Look. Marisol Vega posted her qualifying time from her club pool. Fifty free, twenty-eight seconds. My best is thirty-one. Coach Carter said the top two times make the travel squad." Her thumb hovered over the screen. "I've been stuck on thirty-one all season."

Grayson took the phone. Marisol's post had a photo of her pool, huge and gleaming, with stands on both sides. He looked at it, then at the door that led toward the school pool, then back at the photo. Something didn't line up, but he couldn't see what, because the thing that was wrong wasn't in the picture. It was in the water itself. He walked down the hallway, Dana trailing after him, and counted the tile marks along the pool deck. It was short. Way short. He remembered his uncle griping once about how the Olympics raced in 50-meter pools, called long course, while most school pools were only 25 yards or 25 meters, called short course. He'd barely listened at the time.

"Short course," he said out loud, mostly to himself.

"So?" Dana said.

"So Marisol swam hers long course. Fifty meters. Yours is twenty-five. You can't put those numbers side by side." He turned the phone around so she could see the wide pool again. "A time from a bigger pool can't be compared with your tryout time. It's not the same race."

Dana stared at the photo, then at the pool, then at the clock. It was 3:52. "I have to go warm up," she said, and ran for the locker room, parka flapping. From the gym came the squeak of shoes and Coach Reyes calling for the next group of shooters. Grayson jogged back toward the sound, picking up a ball from the rack.

Grayson spread his French worksheet across the library table and glared at it like it had stolen his lunch. The unit test was Friday, and the speaking part counted double. Worse, his mother had promised that if he passed, they would take his French pen pal, Camille, to a real restaurant when she visited next month. Ordering actual food, out loud, in front of an actual French person. He would rather eat the worksheet.

"Vous désirez?" he muttered at a carton of chocolate milk. The milk did not answer. He tried again. "Je voudrais un sandwich au fromage. Combien ça coûte?" He felt ridiculous talking to dairy, but he kept going, because the words only stuck if he said them out loud.

The tricky part came at the end of every practice meal. His sheet listed foods, prices, and polite words, but it never told him how to ask for the bill. He flipped both pages, then checked the back. Nothing. In English he'd just say "check, please," so he looked up "bill" in the dictionary at the shelf behind him and found "la note." That seemed right. A note, a bill, same idea.

"You look like a detective who lost his suspect," said Priya, dropping into the chair across from him with her own homework.

"I need to ask for the check in French, and my sheet is useless." He showed her his attempted sentence: "La note, s'il vous plaît." "Is that a critique of the worksheet or of my French?"

"Both. But that's a note, like a memo," Priya said. She was the one person in the library who actually spoke some French, thanks to two years of Saturday classes. "My aunt says it wrong too. In a restaurant, it's 'L'addition, s'il vous plaît.'"

"L'addition," Grayson repeated. "Like addition, the math thing? The restaurant adds everything up?"

"Could you paraphrase that for the rest of the class?" Priya said, grinning, but she nodded. "That's how she explained it to me. And don't try 'la facture' either. That's a bill you get in the mail, like for electricity."

Grayson crossed out his sentence and wrote the new one in big letters. Then he stood, held the milk carton like a waiter's tray, and performed the whole meal in one breath. "Bonjour! Je voudrais une pizza et un jus d'orange. Combien ça coûte?" He set the carton down. "Merci. L'addition, s'il vous plaît!"

"Very fancy," Priya said. "Though ordering pizza for a French guest is a little naive. She probably wants crêpes."

"She'll want whatever I can pronounce," Grayson said, and raised the carton in a toast. "L'addition!"

The letter had been waiting on the flour bin all morning, and Charlie finally tore it open while Grandma counted out change for a woman buying honey. Her mom's handwriting slanted across the page: "I hear you two are selling bread at the market now. Wish I could taste it. Last time I tried Grandma's recipe, my loaf came out flat as a brick, and I never figured out why. See if you can do better." Charlie folded the letter into her apron pocket. She had done worse than flat, actually. Two Saturdays ago, tired of standing at the board, she had kneaded for maybe three minutes and quit, and the loaf had risen crooked and torn when she sliced it. She'd let Grandma believe the oven was to blame, a small lie she'd been glad to conceal.

Now the new batch waited under a cloth at the back of the stall, and Charlie pressed her fingers into it. She remembered how Grandma had said, on the very first morning, "Gluten forms when the flour meets the water." Then she'd added, "And kneading makes the gluten stronger and stretchier, so it needs the full ten minutes before it rises." Charlie had nodded and let her mind drift to other things. Ten minutes had seemed like a rule made up to torture bored kids.

The market buzzed around her, the same as every Saturday. The honey woman moved on to the egg stall, where a controversy had been simmering for weeks because Mr. Ruiz claimed the neighboring vendor's "farm fresh" cartons came from a grocery warehouse. Above the awnings, predatory gulls circled and dove at anyone walking off with a pastry. Grandma handed a loaf across the table and said, "Next batch is all yours, Charlie. You did the kneading."

That was the part that stung. Charlie had done the kneading, but she'd cut it short, and she'd said nothing. She looked at the dough, then at her hands, and made up her mind about more than the bread. "Grandma, last time I quit after three minutes. That's why the loaf tore. It wasn't the oven."

Grandna raised one eyebrow, then reached under the cloth and pinched off a piece of dough. "Stretch it," she said. Charlie pulled it gently between her fingers, and it thinned and thinned until light came through it without breaking, like a little window. Ten minutes of kneading had done that. Three minutes had not. She held it up so her grandma could see.

"Well," Grandma said, and there was something in her face between amusement and something older, maybe a memory of her own shortcuts. "Write your mother back and tell her that."

Charlie grinned and reached for the pen under the cash box. "Dear Mom," she said out loud as she wrote, "I know why your loaf was a brick."

Jonathan had exactly eleven minutes before the judges reached his table, and in front of him sat two unmarked jars of clear liquid. Someone had knocked his labels off while squeezing past, and now he couldn't remember which jar was the lemon juice solution and which was the baking soda solution. One of them would turn blue litmus paper red, and one would do the opposite, but he couldn't just guess in front of the judges.

His friend Dex leaned over from the next table, chewing a straw. "Just taste one," Dex whispered.

"They're diluted, and tasting chemicals at a science fair is how you get disqualified," Jonathan muttered. He tore two strips of red litmus paper and two of blue from his kit, because his plan needed both. He dipped a blue strip into jar one and watched.

Nothing happened. He dipped a red strip into the same jar. The paper's edge darkened, creeping from pink toward purple, then unmistakably blue. A base. Jar one was the baking soda solution. Relief washed over him until he glanced up and saw the judges two tables away, one of them an eccentric woman with a telescope pin on her lapel, peering at a project about magnetism.

"Now I have to evaluate which one is stronger," Jonathan said, mostly to himself. He had a jar labeled pH 4 from his earlier trials, and a note that the lemon juice solution measured pH 3. Dex snorted. "pH 3 versus 4? That's basically the same thing. Three, four, who cares?"

"You care," Jonathan said, laying out strips like he was running a tiny algorithm, the same steps every time, no matter what his hands felt like doing. "Each whole step on the pH scale is a tenfold change. So pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4. Ten times. That's the difference between a trickle and a flood." He dipped fresh strips into the lemon jar and his pH 4 reference jar side by side, and the paper in the lemon jar reacted faster, redder, angrier, while the milder solution barely blushed.

The telescope-pin judge stopped at his table. "And what does this demonstration show, young man?"

Jonathan held up both strips, edges damp and red. "The lemon juice is pH 3," he said. "The other one is pH 4. Each whole step on the scale is a tenfold change, so this one is ten times more acidic than that one."

The judge pulled a pen from her coat and made a mark on her clipboard. "Taste anything to find out?"

"No, ma'am. Litmus paper."

She wrote something longer then, and Dex ducked behind his volcano, and Jonathan watched her pen move across the page, line by line, until she looked up and said, "Tell me more about the base."

Katherine sat cross-legged on Priya's bedroom floor with the laptop between them and a shoebox of crumpled dollars and quarters. They had run the lemonade stand all week, their last week before Priya moved to Ohio, and now they had to split the money fairly.

"We can add it by hand," Priya said, but Katherine shook her head. She wanted a real spreadsheet, the kind her older cousin made, with a chart and everything. She typed the days into column A, Monday through Saturday, and the dollar amounts into column B, from B2 down to B10, which was where Saturday's number landed. Then she stared at the empty cell where the total should go. She knew the equals sign came first. She tried typing B2+B3+B4 and kept going until her fingers gave out.

Priya leaned over and pointed at the screen. "My dad does this at work. Try =SUM(B2:B10)." Katherine typed it carefully, colon and all. "The colon marks a range," Priya said. "It grabs every cell from B2 to B10." Katherine pressed Enter, and the total popped up: forty-one dollars and seventy-five cents.

But the shoebox held only thirty-six dollars. Katherine refused to guess. She counted the bills twice to verify the hand total, and it still came up short by five seventy-five. So she tested the formula instead, the way she'd test anything she couldn't see. She clicked on B7, Wednesday, and typed a zero over the five seventy-five that was there. The total dropped by exactly that much. The formula was fine. The hidden cause was somewhere in the numbers themselves.

Then she saw it. The bar chart, tall yellow bars for every day except one, showed Wednesday's bar already tiny before she'd touched anything. Wednesday was the rainy day, the day Priya's little brother Marco had covered the stand alone while they were inside drying off. Priya went pale, called Marco in, and asked him one quiet question. Marco dug into his hoodie pocket and produced five dollars and seventy-five cents in quarters, which he had been saving, he said, for a present for Priya. It was meant to be a going-away surprise.

The consequence of the missing money was a fight that lasted ten minutes and a hug that lasted longer. They took a vote on the chart color, and it was unanimous: yellow, like the lemons. Katherine split the money, half and half, and Priya copied the file onto a flash drive so they could both keep it.

"Send me a new spreadsheet from Ohio," Katherine said. "Every week. Even in winter."

Priya smiled and zipped the drive into her suitcase, right next to Marco's present, still half wrapped.

The clock above the whiteboard showed three minutes left in club, and Brielle's program still wasn't fast enough. Mr. Ruiz had challenged everyone to build a prime checker, and hers worked, but when she typed in a big number like 7919, the little wheel on the screen spun forever. Across the table, her colleague for the day, Deshawn, leaned over.

"Mine's slow too," he said. "Maybe the computer is just old."

"It's not the computer," Brielle said. She scrolled through her loop. "It's the program. We're testing every single number from 2 up. That's thousands of divisions." She highlighted the line: for divisor in range(2, number):. "There has to be a way to magnify the problem, like, zoom in on exactly where we're wasting time."

She tried an experiment. She typed in 15 and added a print statement to show every divisor the program tested. The output spilled down the screen: 2, then 3, then 4, then 5. The answer was 15 is not prime, and 5 had proven it. "Look," she said, pointing. "After 2, it tested 4. Then 6 would come, then 8. But 15 is odd. It can never be divided evenly by an even number, so all of those even divisors are dead ends."

Deshawn frowned at the screen. "Wait. So after we check whether the number is divisible by 2..."

"We only need to test odd divisors," Brielle said, already typing. She changed the range to start at 3 and step by 2, so the loop skipped 4, 6, 8, and everything else that was even. Half the work, gone. She ran it on 7919 and the answer flashed back before she could even blink: 7919 is prime.

"Run it again, run the giant one," Deshawn said, and she typed 104729. Instant answer. They high-fived so hard the mouse skittered off the pad.

Then came the twist. When Mr. Ruiz walked past and glanced at her screen, he smiled and said, "Nice work. Now try 2." Brielle typed it. The program printed 2 is not prime. Her whole body went cold. She and Deshawn burst out laughing, and she grabbed the keyboard to fix the special case before the bell could ring.

"First one to handle 2 and 1 wins," Deshawn said.

"You're on," said Brielle, and hit Enter.

Megan stared at the two jars on the back counter of Mr. Reyes's science classroom. One had held chicken soup sealed tight since Monday, and it still looked like soup. The other, covered only with loose foil, had turned cloudy and smelled like gym socks. Her science fair project was due in nine days, and all she had so far was one good jar and one gross one.

"Your problem is you're guessing," said Deshawn, who was building a volcano two tables over. "You can't just say germs floated in. Did you see them float in?"

That was the trouble. Nobody could see them float in. Megan wrote in her notebook: maybe the soup went bad because something in the air landed on it, not because the soup itself was rotten from the start. It was a guess, but a testable one. If she was right, then broth in a container where the air had to travel through a long, twisting path would stay clean, because the bad stuff in the air would not make it around the bends. If she was wrong, that broth would go bad just like the foil jar.

Mr. Reyes let her stay after class to look through his old science books, and there she found a drawing that made her sit up straight. Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks, and the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck. She read the sentence three times. Someone had tested her exact idea a long time ago, and it had worked.

"It's like a trap," she told Deshawn the next morning, holding up a diagram she had copied. "The neck bends like a snake, and the germs get stuck in the bend. Sealed jar, swan-neck flask, both stay clean. Open jar goes disgusting."

"So your hypothesis was right," Deshawn said. "Somebody just proved it before you were born."

"That's not the point." Megan grabbed a marker and started sketching on her poster board. "The point is I can test it myself. I'll boil broth in three containers. One sealed, one with a bent tube for a neck, one open. If the bent one stays clean, my guess holds up. If it goes bad, I was wrong and I start over." She paused, marker in the air. "It won't go bad."

"Don't be reckless," Deshawn said. "Last time you promised the volcano wouldn't leak, and my protagonist ended up covered in baking soda."

"That was your volcano and your protagonist." Megan taped the diagram to the middle of her board and wrote her hypothesis across the top in careful block letters. She set the three containers on the windowsill where everyone in class could watch them, side by side, and slid a folded card in front of each one. On the third card she wrote a single question mark.

"Nine days," Deshawn said.

"Then we find out."

Elizabeth turned the garden hose on the low dirt slope at the back fence, where her little brother Danny had claimed the whole yard as his construction site and was arguing that his plastic dinosaurs needed a real canyon.

"You can't make one," Danny said. "Canyons are giant. That hose is tiny."

"So was the river that made the Grand Canyon, probably." She didn't actually know if that was true, and it bugged her all through dinner. Afterward she dug through her earth science book until she found the page she'd half-skipped: a Scottish geologist named James Hutton had argued in 1785 that slow, everyday processes like erosion, working over immense time, shaped Earth's surface. She read the sentence twice. No flood, no catastrophe, no dinosaur-destroying drama. Just ordinary water, given millions of years.

The next afternoon she set up the test. She propped a wooden plank at a slant, packed wet dirt along the top, and clamped the hose so a thin trickle ran down the middle. "We leave it on low for two hours," she told Danny. "We check every ten minutes."

At first nothing. The water darkened the dirt and pooled at the bottom, carrying a smear of mud. Danny wandered off to harass the neighbor's cat, a tenant of the garage apartment who tolerated him from the porch steps. But at the twenty-minute check, there was a groove. A shallow one, wobbly, but unmistakable. By forty minutes the groove had deepened and bent where the dirt was softer, and at the base a little fan of mud had spread out, grains the water had carried and dropped.

"It moved the dirt," Danny said, crouching down. "The whole hill is getting eaten."

"Slowly. Like one grain at a time." She crouched beside him. The trickle had done in an hour what Danny thought needed a monster flood, and the only difference she could point to was time. If an hour of hose water carved that, then a river persisting for millions of years, every single day, didn't need to be a monster at all. The canyon felt inevitable, the way a dripping tap eventually fills a bucket.

Danny poked the muddy fan at the bottom with a stick. "So Hutton guy, he just watched water and figured out mountains?"

"Somebody had to actually look, I guess." Elizabeth turned the hose a notch lower, so the trickle was barely a thread, and they sat in the drying grass to see whether the groove would keep growing anyway. Danny laid his largest dinosaur at the top of the slope and said, "Give it a million years, buddy."

Kate sat cross-legged in the desk chair, the house quiet except for the hum of the old computer and the smell of her mother's soup drifting up the stairs. On the screen was a half-written email: an invitation to her thirteenth birthday party, addressed to nobody yet. She had typed all twenty-six names from her class list into a text file, but when she tried pasting them into the To field, she stopped. Last year Marcus had sent a party invite to everyone, and every single address had shown up right there at the top, where anybody could copy them. Kate's dad called it a "chain of everybody knowing everybody's business," and he treated careful email habits like something hereditary, passed down from his own mother, who had always double-locked the front door.

She scrolled through the compose window and noticed a small link that said BCC, next to a link that said CC. CC she knew; her English teacher had used it once when forwarding a reminder about citations for their research papers, and both classes had been able to see each other's addresses. BCC was a mystery. She clicked it, and a new empty field opened below the To line.

Kate reasoned it out the way she reasoned out anything: she tested it. She put her own address in the To field, put her grandmother's address in the BCC field, and wrote "testing, ignore this" in the body. Then she walked to the kitchen, logged in on her mother's laptop, and opened the message that had arrived there. Her own address appeared in the To line. Her grandmother's address appeared in the BCC line, because Mom's laptop was logged in as Grandma sometimes. But when Kate checked the copy that arrived at her own address, there was no BCC line at all, and Grandma's address was nowhere in it.

"BCC," said her brother Dev from the doorway, reading over her shoulder with a cracker in his hand. "Blind carbon copy. The people you put there get the message, but the other recipients can't see their addresses."

"That's what I thought," Kate said, though she hadn't, not for sure. She went back upstairs, past the soup smell and the settling creaks of the evening house, and pasted all twenty-six names into the BCC field. In the To field she typed only her own address, so the email would still look like a proper invitation and not like a message sent to nobody. She added the party details, the time, the request to bring a swimsuit, and a line about the one rule that would govern the whole afternoon: no presents, just food and the pool. Then she pressed send and listened to the little whoosh the old computer made, like a breath let out.

Within a minute, replies began to arrive. Priya wrote "I'M COMING" in all capitals, which Kate knew meant excitement and not shouting, since Priya always wrote that way when she was happy. Leo replied with a single thumbs-up emoji. Kate closed the laptop lid halfway, leaving it open a crack the way she always did, and went down to set the table before her mother called her.

Sofia spread her homework on the library table: one short story, one worksheet, and a pencil she had already sharpened twice. The worksheet asked her to find foreshadowing and symbolism and explain what each suggested. Her friend Marcus dropped into the chair across from her with his own copy of the same story and a bag of pretzels he wasn't supposed to have open.

"I just need to finish and get to soccer by four," Marcus said. He flipped to the last page first. "It's about a guy hunting another guy on an island. Done. I'll write that it was exciting."

"That's not what the sheet asks." Sofia tapped the top line of her paper. "It wants what the story hints at before things happen." She read the first page again, slowly this time. The story was "The Most Dangerous Game," written by Richard Connell in 1924. Early on, a sailor says the place they're heading for is evil, and even mentions that the crew won't go near it. She sat back. Why would sailors fear a random island?

She tried an experiment on Marcus, since he was right there eating pretzels anyway. "Pretend you're a sailor and you hear there's an island called Ship-Trap Island. What would you think?"

Marcus stopped chewing. "I'd think ships get trapped there. I'd steer around it with both hands on the rudder." He shrugged. "Why, is that the answer? Write it down, then I'll copy it."

"No, you won't." She pulled the story toward her and pointed at the name in the text. "Ship-Trap Island. The sailors in the story are scared of it before anything happens to them. The name itself is telling us there's danger waiting there." She wrote that on her sheet, then crossed out her first try, which had been about the ocean, and wrote it again more plainly. "That's foreshadowing. The place name gives away more than the characters realize."

Marcus copied half of it, got bored, and went to find a book about soccer for his reading log, since he needed two more before Friday. Sofia kept reading. Later in the story the general's house sat on a cliff like something watching the sea, and she thought about that too, the way the place itself seemed to radiate a warning the characters kept ignoring. It was vain to expect Marcus to see it, but she didn't mind working alone. When the librarian passed, Sofia asked if the library had anything else by Richard Connell.

"There's a collection in the back," the librarian said. "Same shelf as the adventure stories."

Sofia packed her worksheet, returned Connell's story to the cart, and headed for the back shelf, pencil still behind her ear.

Emily wanted one thing from Tuesday's lab: a graph better than Marcus Delgado's. Marcus had already claimed his rolling ball crossed the table in "about two seconds," which was not a measurement so much as a shrug with numbers attached. Their assignment was to quantify speed using distance and time, then plot distance against time, and Mr. Ruiz had said the neatest graph would hang on the wall until June. June was a long time to look at Marcus Delgado's handwriting.

The trouble was the ball itself. The table was two meters long, marked in chalk every ten centimeters, and the steel ball covered it in less time than Emily could say the word "now." Her stopwatch, borrowed from a drawer of equipment labeled obsolete, probably from the era of chalkboards and dinosaurs, didn't even register half her attempts. Her partner Daisy wrote down dashes where the numbers should go. "We can't graph a dash," Daisy said. "A dash isn't data."

Emily stood there chewing her pencil, which tasted like the lab smelled, vinegar and dust. Then she remembered the science museum from sixth grade. There had been a long wooden ramp exhibit, and a plaque beside it. She had read it twice because she was waiting for her brother to stop playing with the parachute chair. The plaque said Galileo studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps, which slowed the motion enough for him to time it. She hadn't thought about it since. Now she thought about it very hard.

"Gentle ramps," she said. "We lower the angle." They propped one end of a board on a single textbook so it rose barely a finger's width, released the ball at the top, and the ball rolled down at a pace so leisurely Daisy had time to say "go," click the watch, sneeze, and still click stop. They ran it three times, timed it three times, and the numbers came out close enough to plot. Emily drew her graph in sharp pencil: distance up the side, time along the bottom, points landing in a nearly straight line. Behind them, a jar containing some pale preserved organism floated in its fluid, witnessing everything and offering nothing.

They were carrying the board back when Marcus looked over. "Nice ramp," he said. "Too bad the assignment says rolling ball on a flat surface. My graph is straight. Yours is all."

Emily looked at her graph. Her points didn't make a line that leaned uphill. They curved, swept along faster and faster the farther the ball rolled. She was still staring at it when Mr. Ruiz stopped behind her.

"Now that," he said, tapping the curve, "is the most interesting thing anyone's made in here all year. Marcus, come look at what a ramp does."

Clara needed the spreadsheet finished by fourth period, because Mr. Ruiz had promised to hang the class's snack-sale chart in the hallway outside the office. She had typed the snacks into column A, twelve rows of them, and typed how many of each sold into column B. In cell B15 she wrote =SUM(B2:B13) and pressed Enter. The total said 96.

That was wrong. She knew it was wrong before she checked anything, because the whole sale had raised a hundred and eight dollars and every snack cost exactly one dollar. She counted the rows again. Twelve. She read the formula again, letter by letter, and it still said B2 to B13.

"Your chart looks good," said Marcus, leaning over from the next computer. He was already done, his bars tall and even. Hers looked strange too, once she made the bar chart: the bar for pretzels rose high, but the bar for brownies was missing entirely, flat at zero. That gave her an acute suspicion, because the brownie bar was not small, it was absent.

Brownies were the thing they had sold most of. She looked at cell B9, which held the brownie number, 22. She had pasted it from a note the attendance office sent, because she hadn't wanted to retype it. The 22 sat there looking exactly like every other number. But every other number she had typed by hand, and only one bar had vanished.

She clicked on B9. On the far left of the screen, in the little box that showed what the cell held, she saw it: a quotation mark in front of the 22. The number was not a number at all. It was text. And SUM, she now understood, skips cells that hold text, so a number stored as text gets silently left out of the total. Ninety-six plus the missing twenty-two was one hundred and eighteen, which was too much, but that was because she had also pasted the popcorn number, a 4, and ninety-six plus twenty-two minus an extra double-count somewhere was a problem for a moment, until she retyped both cells by hand.

She deleted B9, typed 22 fresh, and pressed Enter. The total jumped to 118. Then she retyped the pasted popcorn cell too, the 4, and watched the total settle at 108, where it belonged. She highlighted the columns again and inserted the bar chart. Twelve bars now, brownies the tallest, the fracture in her data gone so completely it was as if it had never been there.

"Fourth period in five minutes," Marcus said, saving his file.

Clara saved hers, printed the chart, and carried it down the hall to the spot outside the office, where she taped it up and stepped back to look at the brownie bar standing above all the rest.

The big screen at Rosa's Pizza Palace showed the stadium seconds before kickoff, and Theodore had claimed the best seat in the house, the one dead center with an unobstructed view. Around the long table sat his parents, his little sister, and his cousin Matteo, who had flown in that very morning from Italy and had strong opinions about everything, including which toppings counted as credible pizza and which were crimes against dough.

On the screen, the whole stadium suddenly rose in a rolling line, section by section, thousands of arms flung up like a wave crossing an ocean. Theodore shot to his feet and hollered, "Do the wave!" His sister stood up, then his dad, and soon half the restaurant was bouncing up and down like popcorn in a hot vessel. Matteo just laughed and shook his head.

"You call it the wave," Matteo said. "We call it the Mexican wave."

"You're making that up," Theodore said. "It's just the wave. Everybody calls it the wave." Matteo shrugged in that infuriating way of his and went back to his slice. Theodore could not let this go. It felt like being told the sky was called something else in another country, which, now that he thought about it, was exactly the kind of thing that might be true. He decided to test it. He pulled out the family tablet in the corner by the arcade games and searched, half expecting Matteo to have invented the phrase as a joke, because Matteo's jokes thrived on Theodore believing them.

The search results loaded, and Theodore read them twice. The wave had become known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, and that was exactly why so many English speakers outside North America called it the Mexican wave. Matteo had not made it up. Theodore walked back to the table slowly, the way a detective delivers bad news.

"I owe you a meatball," Theodore said, sliding half of one onto Matteo's plate. "The Mexican wave is a real thing. It got famous at the World Cup in Mexico, and people outside North America actually call it that." Matteo grinned and raised his soda like a trophy. On the screen, the crowd did another wave, and this time Theodore stood up first, shouting, "Mexican wave, everybody! We're doing it the international way!" His little sister stood up so fast she knocked over the parmesan shaker, and Matteo caught it one-handed without even looking away from the goal.

Naomi sat cross-legged in the window seat with the paperback propped against her knees, a pencil behind her ear, and a legal pad on the cushion beside her. Monday's English assignment was one page of Romeo and Juliet, every speech paraphrased into modern English, and she had been staring at Juliet's lines for twenty minutes.

"'This precious book of love," she read, "'this unbound lover, to beautify him, only lacks a cover.'" She wrote "book of love" and crossed it out. What did that even mean? Worse was the next line, where Juliet said the lover "hath no wit." Hath. She flipped to the page Mrs. Okafor had assigned and found hath again, and doth, and saith, scattered through the speeches like typos.

Her brother Dev leaned into the doorway, basketball under one arm. "You're talking to yourself."

"I'm paraphrasing."

"Sounds painful." He came in anyway and dropped onto the cushions. He grabbed the legal pad and read her half-finished line aloud. "'The book of love needs a jacket'? That's terrible."

"Give it back." She snatched the pad, then stopped, tapping the pencil on the page. Dev was in fifth grade and useless for Shakespeare, but he was useful for something else. "Dev. I say a word, you say what it sounds like. Doth."

"Doth." He frowned. "Like... does?"

"Hath."

"Has? Hath, has. Hey, that actually works." He leaned over the book, interested now. "So it's not broken English?"

She scanned the page, hunting for more of them, testing each one. Speaketh, speak. Knoweth, know. It wasn't random. The words ending in th were all just ordinary verbs, and once she read them that way the sentences stopped sounding like fog and started sounding like people talking.
